parts.title: 大問1 短文の語句空所補充
parts.desc: 1〜2文の空所に入る難しい単語・句動詞を4つから選ぶ
parts.tip: まず文全体を読み、空所の語が「良い意味か悪い意味か」「強めか弱めか」を決める。セミコロンや because・although の後ろが言い換えの手がかり。知らない語は接頭辞（in- / dis- / ex-）と語根から消去法で絞る。
parts.intro: Read each sentence and choose the word or phrase from the four choices that best completes it.

questions.q: The committee's report was so ____ that even experts struggled to follow it; its main arguments were buried under pages of technical detail and unexplained abbreviations.
choices: candid
frugal
placid
abstruse
questions.why: abstruse＝「難解な」。専門家でも追えない、細部と略語に埋もれている、という説明と合う。candid（率直な）、frugal（質素な）、placid（穏やかな）は報告書の分かりにくさを表さない。

questions.q: After months of negotiation, the two firms finally signed a deal, but analysts warned that the ____ agreement could collapse if either side changed its priorities.
choices: lucid
tenuous
opulent
verbose
questions.why: tenuous＝「もろい・根拠の弱い」。どちらかの方針が変われば崩れかねない、という警告と合う。lucid（明快な）、opulent（豪華な）、verbose（言葉数の多い）は「崩れやすさ」を表さない。

questions.q: The novelist was famously ____ in interviews, often answering long questions with a single word and refusing to discuss anything about her private life.
choices: gregarious
voracious
taciturn
pliant
questions.why: taciturn＝「無口な」。長い質問に一語で答える、私生活を話さない、と合う。gregarious（社交的な）は逆。voracious（貪欲な）、pliant（従順な）は合わない。

questions.q: Dr. Hale tried to ____ his theory with data from three separate studies, but critics argued that the samples were far too small to prove anything.
choices: obfuscate
relinquish
corroborate
castigate
questions.why: corroborate＝「（証拠で）裏付ける」。3つの研究のデータで、しかし標本が小さすぎて証明にならない、と続く。obfuscate（わざと分かりにくくする）、relinquish（手放す）、castigate（厳しく非難する）は合わない。

questions.q: Although the union leader seemed ____ at first, refusing to consider any form of compromise, he eventually agreed to a modest pay increase for workers.
choices: magnanimous
intransigent
ebullient
gullible
questions.why: intransigent＝「妥協しない・頑固な」。どんな妥協も拒む、と言い換えている。magnanimous（寛大な）は逆。ebullient（元気あふれる）、gullible（だまされやすい）は合わない。

questions.q: Heavy snow ____ the climbers' progress throughout the afternoon, and they reached the mountain hut nearly three hours later than they had planned.
choices: enunciated
exonerated
impeded
emulated
questions.why: impede＝「妨げる・遅らせる」。雪のせいで3時間遅れた、という結果と合う。enunciate（はっきり発音する）、exonerate（無実を証明する）、emulate（見習う）は合わない。

questions.q: Paul's apology struck his colleagues as ____; he had made exactly the same promise twice before and had never actually changed his behavior.
choices: disingenuous
indelible
impeccable
incessant
questions.why: disingenuous＝「不誠実な・本心でない」。同じ約束を2回破っている、という根拠と合う。indelible（消えない）、impeccable（非の打ちどころがない）、incessant（絶え間ない）は合わない。

questions.q: Years of ____ spending left the family with almost no savings, so they were forced to sell their vacation home when Mr. Lowe lost his job.
choices: austere
tacit
nascent
profligate
questions.why: profligate＝「浪費的な」。貯金がほとんど無くなった原因になる。austere（切り詰めた）は逆。tacit（暗黙の）、nascent（生まれたばかりの）は spending を説明しない。

questions.q: The professor's lecture contained several ____ remarks about rival researchers, and a number of students later complained that the comments had been unprofessional.
choices: disparaging
exculpatory
conciliatory
salubrious
questions.why: disparaging＝「見くびった・けなすような」。学生がプロらしくないと苦情を言った、と合う。exculpatory（無罪を示す）、conciliatory（なだめるような）、salubrious（健康に良い）は合わない。

questions.q: When the company's sales began to ____ last year, the board replaced the chief executive and announced an ambitious plan to enter overseas markets.
choices: coalesce
reverberate
germinate
dwindle
questions.why: dwindle＝「次第に減る」。社長交代と海外進出の計画、という立て直しの対応と合う。coalesce（合体する）、reverberate（反響する）、germinate（発芽する）は売上に使わない。

questions.q: The mediator managed to ____ the tension in the room by making a joke about the broken air conditioner, and the talks continued calmly after that.
choices: exacerbate
emancipate
encapsulate
defuse
questions.why: defuse＝「（緊張・危機を）和らげる」。冗談の後、話し合いが落ち着いて続いた。exacerbate（悪化させる）は逆。emancipate（解放する）、encapsulate（要約する）は合わない。

questions.q: The documentary was criticized for its ____ treatment of a complex scientific debate, presenting only one side and ignoring decades of contrary evidence.
choices: tendentious
meticulous
venerable
sonorous
questions.why: tendentious＝「偏った・特定の主張に肩入れした」。一方の側だけを見せ、反対の証拠を無視した。meticulous（細心の）、venerable（尊い）、sonorous（よく響く）は批判の理由にならない。

questions.q: The hotel's ____ lobby, with its marble floors, crystal chandeliers, and gold-framed mirrors, impressed guests the moment they walked through the doors.
choices: opulent
dilapidated
austere
rudimentary
questions.why: opulent＝「豪華な」。大理石の床・シャンデリア・金縁の鏡、という例と合う。dilapidated（荒れ果てた）、austere（簡素な）、rudimentary（初歩的な）は逆の印象。

questions.q: Although Mr. Grant had ____ his support for the project at the first meeting, he changed his mind after reading the final budget and voted against it.
choices: dispelled
abdicated
extricated
avowed
questions.why: avow＝「公言する」。最初は支持を表明 → 予算を見て反対、という Although の対比。dispel（払いのける）、abdicate（退位する・放棄する）、extricate（救い出す）は support と組まない。

questions.q: Dr. Moreno was ____ by her failed experiments; instead of giving up, she redesigned her equipment and began a new series of trials the following week.
choices: undaunted
incensed
belittled
encumbered
questions.why: undaunted＝「ひるまない」。あきらめずに翌週また始めた、と合う。incensed（激怒した）、belittled（けなされた）、encumbered（重荷を負った）は instead of giving up とつながらない。

questions.q: Critics ____ the director for casting inexperienced actors in the main roles, saying that their stiff performances ruined an otherwise excellent script.
choices: commended
vindicated
lambasted
placated
questions.why: lambaste＝「酷評する」。演技が脚本を台無しにした、という批判と合う。commend（ほめる）は逆。vindicate（正しさを証明する）、placate（なだめる）も合わない。

questions.q: To ____ the risk of mold, the museum keeps its rare manuscripts in special rooms where both the temperature and the humidity are carefully controlled.
choices: aggravate
mitigate
emulate
extrapolate
questions.why: mitigate＝「（危険・害を）和らげる」。温度と湿度を管理するのはカビの危険を減らすため。aggravate（悪化させる）は逆。emulate（見習う）、extrapolate（推定する）は合わない。

questions.q: Jenny's ____ curiosity led her to read everything she could find about deep-sea creatures, from picture books for children to graduate-level textbooks.
choices: impassive
insatiable
infallible
innocuous
questions.why: insatiable＝「飽くことのない」。見つけた物は絵本から大学院の教科書まで全部読んだ。impassive（無表情な）、infallible（絶対に誤らない）、innocuous（無害な）は好奇心の強さを表さない。

questions.q: The economist's model rested on a ____ assumption: that all consumers behave rationally, an idea that research in psychology has repeatedly shown to be false.
choices: sanguine
opportune
fallacious
palatable
questions.why: fallacious＝「誤った」。心理学の研究で何度も否定された、と続く。sanguine（楽観的な）、opportune（時宜を得た）、palatable（口に合う・受け入れやすい）は「誤り」の意味にならない。

questions.q: After the factory closed, the once-busy town fell into a long period of economic ____, with shops boarded up and young people moving away.
choices: proliferation
exuberance
malaise
remuneration
questions.why: malaise＝「（経済などの）不振・沈滞」。店が閉まり若者が出て行く様子と合う。proliferation（急増）、exuberance（活気）、remuneration（報酬）は合わない。

questions.q: The company tried to ____ public criticism of its new product by offering free repairs, but many customers had already switched to rival brands.
choices: incite
exalt
emanate
deflect
questions.why: deflect criticism＝「批判をかわす」。無料修理という対策と合う。incite（あおる）は逆。exalt（称える）、emanate（発する。自動詞）は合わない。

questions.q: Engineers spent several weeks trying to ____ the cause of the software failure, eventually tracing it to a single line of outdated code.
choices: ameliorate
promulgate
ascertain
recuperate
questions.why: ascertain＝「（事実を）突き止める」。原因を探し、1行のコードにたどり着いた。ameliorate（改善する）、promulgate（公布する）、recuperate（回復する）は the cause と組まない。

questions.q: Many first-time visitors find the old city's ____ alleyways confusing; without a good map, it is easy to walk in circles for an hour or more.
choices: pristine
sedentary
labyrinthine
perennial
questions.why: labyrinthine＝「迷路のような」。地図が無いと同じ所を回ってしまう、と合う。pristine（汚れていない）、sedentary（座りがちな）、perennial（長年続く）は道を説明しない。

questions.q: Although the position was ____, offering a high salary and generous annual bonuses, Kenji resigned after a year because he found the work unfulfilling.
choices: lucrative
frivolous
ominous
clandestine
questions.why: lucrative＝「もうかる」。高い給料とボーナス、と言い換えている。frivolous（軽薄な）、ominous（不吉な）、clandestine（秘密の）は給料の良さを表さない。

questions.q: The young biologist's findings were ____ by many of her peers at first, but within a decade her theory had become widely accepted in the field.
choices: lauded
derided
augmented
annexed
questions.why: deride＝「あざける・ばかにする」。but 以下の「後に広く受け入れられた」と対比になる。lauded（称賛された）では対比にならない。augmented（増やされた）、annexed（併合された）は合わない。

questions.q: The guide warned the tourists that the river was ____ in several places and told them not to cross without holding firmly onto the rope.
choices: placid
treacherous
arid
docile
questions.why: treacherous＝「（見かけによらず）危険な」。ロープにつかまって渡れ、という警告と合う。placid（穏やかな）は逆。arid（乾燥した）、docile（おとなしい）も合わない。

questions.q: The two firms decided to ____ their research departments, hoping that combining their expertise would speed up the development of new medicines.
choices: fragment
amalgamate
emancipate
decimate
questions.why: amalgamate＝「合併する・統合する」。combining their expertise（専門知識を合わせる）と同じ意味。fragment（分割する）は逆。emancipate（解放する）、decimate（大量に減らす）は合わない。

questions.q: The old theater was ____ with mice that had nested inside its walls, so the owners closed it for several weeks while pest-control workers dealt with the problem.
choices: infested
imbued
endowed
adorned
questions.why: be infested with ～＝「（害虫などが）はびこっている」。駆除の間閉館した。imbued（染み込んだ）、endowed（恵まれた）、adorned（飾られた）は害のある物には使わない。

questions.q: Rachel's ____ comments about the new logo hurt her colleague's feelings, though she later insisted that she had only been trying to be honest.
choices: benign
effusive
cordial
caustic
questions.why: caustic＝「辛辣な」。相手を傷つけた、正直に言っただけだと弁解した、と合う。benign（優しい）、cordial（心のこもった）は逆。effusive（感情をあふれさせた・大げさにほめる）も人を傷つけない。

questions.q: Ms. Rivera was ____ to accept the promotion at first, worried that the extra responsibilities would leave her very little time for her young family.
choices: privy
akin
rife
loath
questions.why: be loath to do＝「～するのに気が進まない」。家族との時間が減るのを心配した。privy to（～を内々に知る）、akin to（～に似た）、rife with（～だらけの）は後ろに動詞の原形を取れない。

questions.q: The small bakery has developed a ____ following; on weekends, customers line up outside before dawn to buy its famous sourdough bread.
choices: fleeting
fervent
nominal
desultory
questions.why: fervent＝「熱烈な」。夜明け前から並ぶ客、という例と合う。fleeting（つかの間の）、nominal（名ばかりの）、desultory（気まぐれな）は熱心さと逆の意味。

questions.q: Because the instructions were so ____, half of the participants misunderstood what they were supposed to do and had to repeat the experiment.
choices: nebulous
explicit
punctual
prolific
questions.why: nebulous＝「あいまいな・漠然とした」。半数が誤解した原因になる。explicit（明確な）は逆。punctual（時間を守る）、prolific（多作の）は指示を説明しない。

questions.q: The chef's new menu was a ____ success; within a month, reservations had doubled and critics were praising it in several national magazines.
choices: marginal
resounding
specious
perfunctory
questions.why: a resounding success＝「大成功」。予約が倍、全国誌でほめられた。marginal（わずかな）、perfunctory（おざなりの）は成功の大きさを表さない。specious（もっともらしいがうそっぽい）も合わない。

questions.q: The sale of the house almost ____ when the buyer discovered serious problems with the roof, but the owner agreed to lower the price by ten percent.
choices: drew up
set off
fell through
turned in
questions.why: fall through＝「（計画・取引が）だめになる」。屋根の問題で売買が流れかけた → 値下げで助かった。draw up（作成する）、set off（出発する）、turn in（提出する・寝る）は合わない。

questions.q: Mark's parents told him he could not keep ____ his decision about which university to attend, since the application deadline was only a week away.
choices: bringing about
running over
handing out
putting off
questions.why: put off＝「先延ばしにする」。締め切りが1週間後なので、決断を延ばせない。bring about（引き起こす）、run over（ひく・ざっと見直す）、hand out（配る）は合わない。

questions.q: The excitement over the new phone soon ____ when users discovered that its battery lasted only half a day and that the camera often froze.
choices: chipped in
wore off
stood out
pulled through
questions.why: wear off＝「（効果・感情が）薄れる」。電池が半日しかもたないと分かり、熱が冷めた。chip in（お金を出し合う）、stand out（目立つ）、pull through（切り抜ける）は合わない。

questions.q: After working for a large bakery chain for twelve years, Alan finally had enough savings to ____ on his own and open a small shop downtown.
choices: strike out
bear out
pore over
fend off
questions.why: strike out on one's own＝「独立する」。大手を辞めて自分の店を開く。bear out（裏付ける）、pore over（熟読する）、fend off（撃退する）は on one's own と組まない。

questions.q: The speaker ____ on minor details of the project's history for so long that she had no time left to explain its most important results.
choices: embarked
reneged
encroached
dwelt
questions.why: dwell on ～＝「～についてくどくど話す」。細かい話に時間を使い、肝心の結果を話す時間が無くなった。embark on（乗り出す）、renege on（約束を破る）、encroach on（侵害する）は合わない。

questions.q: The marketing team had to ____ a completely new campaign in just two days after the original one was canceled at the last minute.
choices: throw together
write off
stave off
look down
questions.why: throw together＝「急ごしらえで作る」。2日で新しいキャンペーンを作った。write off（帳消しにする・見切る）、stave off（食い止める）、look down（見下ろす）は合わない。

questions.q: When the hikers ran out of food on the third day, they had to ____ on the few energy bars that one member had packed at the bottom of his bag.
choices: cash in
hold out
fall back
chime in
questions.why: fall back on ～＝「（いざという時に）～に頼る」。食料が尽きて、残りの栄養バーに頼った。cash in on（～で利益を得る）、hold out on（～に隠し事をする）、chime in（口をはさむ）は合わない。

questions.q: The new manager's ____ manner quickly put the nervous staff at ease; she greeted everyone by name and laughed easily at her own small mistakes.
choices: pompous
brusque
affable
furtive
questions.why: affable＝「気さくな・愛想のよい」。緊張した職員を安心させ、名前で挨拶し、自分の失敗を笑う、と合う。brusque（ぶっきらぼうな）、pompous（尊大な）、furtive（こそこそした）は逆の印象。

questions.q: Since the fish-canning factory closed, the once-busy harbor village has become almost ____, and most of its houses now stand empty for eleven months of the year.
choices: boisterous
congested
verdant
desolate
questions.why: desolate＝「人けのない・荒涼とした」。工場が閉まり、家が1年の大半空いている。boisterous（騒がしい）、congested（混雑した）は逆。verdant（緑豊かな）は人の少なさを表さない。

questions.q: Although the evidence against the theory was ____, a few researchers continued to defend it, insisting that every one of the experiments had been poorly designed.
choices: specious
tentative
negligible
incontrovertible
questions.why: incontrovertible＝「反論の余地のない」。Although があるので「証拠は強いのに、一部の人は擁護を続けた」という対比。specious（もっともらしいだけの）、tentative（仮の）、negligible（ごくわずかな）では対比にならない。

questions.q: The airline tried to ____ passengers' fears about its new aircraft by publishing detailed safety records and inviting journalists to tour its maintenance center.
choices: assuage
substantiate
insinuate
provoke
questions.why: assuage＝「（不安・苦痛を）和らげる」。安全記録の公開や見学会で不安を和らげる。provoke（引き起こす）、substantiate（裏付ける）は不安を強める方向で逆。insinuate（遠回しに言う）は fears と組まない。

questions.q: Facing a sharp drop in ticket sales, the orchestra was forced to ____ its touring schedule, canceling concerts in six cities and postponing a planned trip abroad.
choices: augment
embellish
curtail
reiterate
questions.why: curtail＝「削減する・切り詰める」。6都市の公演中止と海外公演の延期が具体例。augment（増やす）は逆。embellish（飾り立てる）、reiterate（繰り返す）は合わない。

questions.q: After the company was sold, the founder's once-central role was ____ to that of an occasional adviser, and he was no longer invited to board meetings.
choices: elevated
relegated
ratified
reinstated
questions.why: relegate A to B＝「Aを（低い地位・役割）に追いやる」。時々の相談役になり、役員会にも呼ばれない。elevated（高められた）、reinstated（復帰させられた）は逆。ratified（批准された）は役割には使わない。

questions.q: Fans accused the club's owners of ____ the team's early advantage; after leading the league in May, it made a series of poor signings and finished eighth.
choices: bequeathing
consolidating
squandering
reclaiming
questions.why: squander＝「（機会・お金を）無駄にする」。5月は首位だったのに、下手な補強で8位に終わった。consolidating（固める）は逆。bequeathing（遺贈する）、reclaiming（取り戻す）は合わない。

questions.q: Thanks to a long vaccination campaign, the disease has been almost entirely ____ in the region, with only two cases reported in the past decade.
choices: proliferated
incubated
eradicated
quarantined
questions.why: eradicate＝「根絶する」。予防接種のおかげで10年に2例だけ。proliferate（急増する）は逆。incubate（培養する）、quarantine（隔離する）は「ほぼ完全に」「10年で2例」と合わない。

questions.q: The coach warned his players that arguing with referees could ____ their chances of being selected for the national squad, since the selectors valued discipline above all.
choices: jeopardize
validate
enhance
commemorate
questions.why: jeopardize＝「危うくする」。選考では規律を最も重んじるので、審判への抗議は不利になる。enhance（高める）は逆。validate（正当と認める）、commemorate（記念する）は合わない。

questions.q: To ____ her application for the research post, Dr. Chen included letters of recommendation from three senior scientists who had supervised her work.
choices: disavow
undermine
bolster
forsake
questions.why: bolster＝「強化する・後押しする」。推薦状3通で応募を強くする。undermine（弱める）は逆。disavow（否認する）、forsake（見捨てる）は合わない。

questions.q: Before signing the lease, Ms. Walsh asked her lawyer to ____ every clause, because a friend had warned her about hidden fees in similar contracts.
choices: obliterate
scrutinize
extol
eulogize
questions.why: scrutinize＝「綿密に調べる」。隠れた手数料が心配で、条項を一つ残らず調べてもらう。obliterate（消し去る）、eulogize（賛辞を述べる）、extol（ほめたたえる）は契約書の確認に合わない。

questions.q: The pilot was formally ____ by the airline for leaving the cockpit without informing his co-pilot, although no passengers were put in danger by his mistake.
choices: commended
emboldened
pacified
reprimanded
questions.why: reprimand＝「（正式に）叱責する」。副操縦士に知らせず操縦席を離れた、というミスへの処分。commended（ほめられた）は逆。pacified（なだめられた）、emboldened（大胆にされた）は合わない。

questions.q: Several employees said they had been ____ into working unpaid overtime, claiming that their manager had hinted that anyone who refused would lose their annual bonus.
choices: absolved
coerced
indulged
deterred
questions.why: coerce A into doing＝「Aに無理やり～させる」。断るとボーナスが無くなるとほのめかされた。absolve（免除する）、indulge（甘やかす）、deter（思いとどまらせる。from を取る）は into working と合わない。

questions.q: Many students choose to ____ a summer vacation and do an internship instead, believing that the work experience will give them an advantage when they apply for jobs.
choices: forgo
procure
emulate
relish
questions.why: forgo＝「（楽しみを）あきらめる・なしで済ませる」。休暇の代わりにインターンをする（instead）。relish（楽しむ）は逆。procure（手に入れる）、emulate（見習う）は instead とつながらない。

questions.q: The university ____ its decision to raise tuition fees after thousands of students and parents signed a petition and several major donors expressed concern.
choices: reiterated
rescinded
implemented
exacerbated
questions.why: rescind＝「（決定を）撤回する」。署名と大口寄付者の懸念を受けて取り消した。reiterate（繰り返し述べる）、implement（実行する）は流れが逆。exacerbate（悪化させる）は decision と組まない。

questions.q: The storyteller ____ the young audience for over an hour; not a single child moved or spoke until the final words of the tale had been spoken.
choices: enthralled
alienated
berated
sedated
questions.why: enthrall＝「魅了する」。1時間以上、子どもが誰も動かず話さなかった。alienate（遠ざける）、berate（叱りつける）は逆。sedate（鎮静剤で落ち着かせる）は語り手の行為に合わない。

questions.q: Smartphones have become so ____ that it is now difficult to find a café or a train carriage in which most people are not staring at a screen.
choices: clandestine
obsolete
esoteric
ubiquitous
questions.why: ubiquitous＝「どこにでもある」。カフェにも電車にもあふれている。obsolete（時代遅れの）、esoteric（一部の人にしか分からない）、clandestine（秘密の）は逆の意味。

questions.q: Fashion trends on social media tend to be ____; a style that seems to be everywhere one month is often completely forgotten by the next.
choices: ephemeral
inveterate
immutable
perennial
questions.why: ephemeral＝「つかの間の・はかない」。翌月には忘れられる。perennial（長く続く）、inveterate（根深い）、immutable（不変の）はどれも逆。

questions.q: The inspector gave the building only a ____ glance before approving it, and serious problems with the wiring were not discovered until several years later.
choices: meticulous
prolonged
cursory
scathing
questions.why: cursory＝「ざっとした・おざなりの」。ちらっと見ただけで承認し、配線の問題が見落とされた。meticulous（細心の）、prolonged（長時間の）は逆。scathing（痛烈な）は承認と合わない。

questions.q: Rather than insisting on an ideal solution, the committee took a ____ approach, choosing the plan that could be completed within the existing budget and timeframe.
choices: dogmatic
pragmatic
quixotic
whimsical
questions.why: pragmatic＝「実際的な」。理想にこだわらず、予算と期間内でできる案を選んだ。dogmatic（独断的な）、quixotic（非現実的な理想を追う）、whimsical（気まぐれな）は逆。

questions.q: Many skills that were once essential for office workers, such as taking notes in shorthand, have become almost ____ as new technologies have taken over those tasks.
choices: contagious
indispensable
innate
obsolete
questions.why: obsolete＝「すたれた・時代遅れの」。新しい技術がその仕事を引き継いだ。indispensable（不可欠な）は逆。innate（生まれつきの）、contagious（伝染性の）は合わない。

questions.q: After winning the championship three years in a row, the team became ____, and its players stopped training as hard as they had in previous seasons.
choices: diligent
complacent
destitute
indignant
questions.why: complacent＝「現状に満足しきった・油断した」。3連覇の後、練習の手を抜いた。diligent（勤勉な）は逆。destitute（極貧の）、indignant（憤慨した）は合わない。

questions.q: The taxi driver was so ____ that Helen could hardly get a word in; he talked nonstop about his family, his hobbies, and the city's history for the entire journey.
choices: reticent
sullen
garrulous
laconic
questions.why: garrulous＝「おしゃべりな」。口をはさめないほど、ずっと話していた。reticent（口数の少ない）、laconic（言葉数の少ない）は逆。sullen（不機嫌な）も合わない。

questions.q: In his bright orange jacket, Leo was ____ among the crowd of guests in dark suits, and several people asked whether he had come to the wrong event.
choices: conspicuous
indistinguishable
incognito
unobtrusive
questions.why: conspicuous＝「目立つ」。暗いスーツの中で明るいオレンジの上着、会場違いかと聞かれた。indistinguishable（見分けがつかない）、incognito（お忍びの）、unobtrusive（控えめな）は逆。

questions.q: The young architect's ____ design, which placed a glass concert hall on top of an old grain warehouse, shocked the judges, but it eventually won the competition.
choices: derivative
audacious
mundane
insipid
questions.why: audacious＝「大胆な」。古い倉庫の上にガラスのホール、という型破りな案で審査員を驚かせた。derivative（独創性のない）、mundane（平凡な）、insipid（面白みのない）は逆。

questions.q: Patients often feel ____ for several days after the operation, so the hospital advises them not to drive or return to work until their energy has fully returned.
choices: vivacious
exuberant
lethargic
jubilant
questions.why: lethargic＝「だるい・無気力な」。体力が戻るまで運転や仕事は控える。vivacious（快活な）、exuberant（元気いっぱいの）、jubilant（大喜びの）は逆。

questions.q: A ____ negotiator, Ms. Ito refused to give up on the deal, even after the other company had rejected her proposals four times in a single month.
choices: capricious
feeble
diffident
tenacious
questions.why: tenacious＝「粘り強い」。1か月に4回断られても諦めない。capricious（気まぐれな）、feeble（弱々しい）、diffident（自信のない）は逆。

questions.q: The success of the first electric ferries gave fresh ____ to the port authority's plan to replace its entire fleet with low-emission vessels by the end of the decade.
choices: hindrance
impetus
deterrent
pretext
questions.why: impetus＝「はずみ・勢い」。最初の成功が計画を後押しした。hindrance（妨げ）、deterrent（抑止するもの）は逆。pretext（口実）は give fresh ～ to the plan と合わない。

questions.q: There is a ____ of qualified nurses in many rural areas, and hospitals there often have to rely on temporary staff from distant cities.
choices: glut
dearth
plethora
surplus
questions.why: dearth＝「不足」。遠くの都市の臨時職員に頼るほど足りない。glut（供給過剰）、plethora（過多）、surplus（余剰）はどれも逆。

questions.q: Having missed the last ferry and with his phone battery dead, Owen found himself in a real ____ and had to knock on doors until someone offered him a bed.
choices: windfall
reverie
sanctuary
predicament
questions.why: predicament＝「苦境」。最終フェリーを逃し、電話も使えない。windfall（思わぬ幸運）、reverie（空想）、sanctuary（避難所）は状況に合わない。

questions.q: Because the explorer's diaries were lost, any account of his final weeks is largely ____, based only on a few letters and the memories of his local guides.
choices: conjecture
dogma
certainty
verification
questions.why: conjecture＝「推測」。日記が無く、手紙数通と記憶だけが頼り。certainty（確実なこと）、verification（検証）は逆。dogma（教義）は合わない。

questions.q: The film received the festival's highest ____, and its director was praised for telling a moving story with almost no dialogue.
choices: censure
stipend
accolade
ultimatum
questions.why: accolade＝「栄誉・賞賛」。最高の賞を受け、監督がほめられた。censure（非難）は逆。stipend（給付金）、ultimatum（最後通告）は合わない。

questions.q: For years, Kate suffered from ____ headaches that sometimes kept her in bed for days at a time, until a new treatment finally brought them under control.
choices: negligible
invigorating
debilitating
therapeutic
questions.why: debilitating＝「体をひどく弱らせる」。何日も寝込むほどの頭痛。invigorating（元気づける）、negligible（取るに足りない）は逆。therapeutic（治療の）は頭痛を説明しない。

questions.q: The two companies still need to ____ a few remaining differences over pricing before the merger agreement can be signed next month.
choices: lash out
bow out
hold up
iron out
questions.why: iron out＝「（問題・食い違いを）解消する」。契約の前に価格の食い違いをなくす。lash out（激しく非難する）、bow out（身を引く）、hold up（遅らせる）は differences を解消する意味にならない。

questions.q: Before her transfer to the Madrid office, Lucy took evening classes to ____ her Spanish, which she had hardly used since graduating from university.
choices: brush up on
measure up to
crack down on
face up to
questions.why: brush up on＝「（さびついた技能を）磨き直す」。大学以来ほとんど使っていないスペイン語。crack down on（取り締まる）、measure up to（期待にこたえる）、face up to（直視する）は合わない。

questions.q: The annual report was criticized for ____ the project's serious delays, mentioning them only briefly in a footnote on the final page.
choices: glossing over
dwelling on
zeroing in on
living up to
questions.why: gloss over＝「（都合の悪い点を）さらっと流す・ごまかす」。最後のページの脚注で少し触れただけ。dwell on（くどくど話す）、zero in on（的を絞る）は逆。live up to（期待にこたえる）は合わない。

questions.q: When the debate over the new stadium grew heated, several local business owners ____ with their own views, arguing that it would bring more visitors to the area.
choices: made off
tapered off
dropped out
weighed in
questions.why: weigh in (with ～)＝「（議論に）意見を出して加わる」。地元の事業者が意見を述べた。taper off（次第に減る）、drop out（脱落する）、make off（逃げ去る）は with their own views と合わない。

questions.q: We can't ____ good weather for the outdoor festival in April, so we should rent a few large tents just in case it rains.
choices: make up for
bank on
stand up for
look up to
questions.why: bank on＝「～を当てにする」。天気を当てにできないので、雨に備えてテントを借りる。make up for（埋め合わせる）、look up to（尊敬する）、stand up for（擁護する）は合わない。

questions.q: The bank plans to ____ paper statements over the next two years, gradually encouraging all of its customers to switch to online banking instead.
choices: pass up
chalk up
mull over
phase out
questions.why: phase out＝「段階的に廃止する」。2年かけて少しずつオンラインに切り替える。pass up（見送る）、chalk up（記録する）、mull over（じっくり考える）は合わない。

questions.q: With its debts rising quickly, the company had no choice but to ____ spending, freezing new hires and cutting its travel budget in half.
choices: rein in
scale up
ramp up
dish out
questions.why: rein in＝「（支出などを）抑える」。採用凍結と出張費の半減。scale up（規模を拡大する）、ramp up（増やす）は逆。dish out（配る）は合わない。

parts.title: 大問2 長文の語句空所補充
parts.desc: 約350語の説明文・評論文の空所3つに入る語句を4つから選ぶ
parts.tip: 空所の後ろの1〜2文（具体例・言い換え）が根拠になることが多い。段落の頭の空所は「前の段落と逆か・続きか」を先に決める。選択肢は本文の語を使った引っかけが多いので、意味で選ぶ。
parts.intro: Read each passage and choose the best phrase from among the four choices for each numbered blank.

sets.passage:
Too Many Choices?

For decades, economists took it for granted that having more options could only benefit consumers. If a shopper finds a selection too large, the reasoning went, she can simply ignore the items that do not interest her and focus on the rest. In one frequently cited experiment, however, this assumption appeared to break down. Researchers set up a tasting stand in a grocery store that offered either six or twenty-four varieties of olive oil. Although the larger display attracted more visitors, shoppers who saw only six varieties were far more likely to buy a bottle. Many of those who stopped at the larger display tasted several oils, hesitated, and walked away empty-handed. The researchers concluded that an abundance of options can ( 1 ).

The idea, which became known as "choice overload," quickly spread beyond the university. Business consultants advised companies to trim their product lines, and some employers reduced the number of investment funds offered in their retirement-savings plans. Popular books on decision-making cited the study as evidence that modern consumers were suffering from too much freedom. ( 2 ), the phenomenon proved surprisingly difficult to reproduce. When other research teams repeated similar experiments with products ranging from chocolates to music downloads, many found that larger assortments had little or no negative effect on purchases. One review that combined the results of dozens of studies concluded that, on average, the effect was close to zero.

This does not mean that choice overload is simply a myth. Rather, many researchers now believe that it appears only under particular conditions. People are most likely to feel overwhelmed when the options are difficult to compare, when they are under time pressure, or when they ( 3 ). A wine expert choosing from a list of fifty bottles, for example, can quickly narrow down the possibilities by region and grape, whereas a beginner may find the same list bewildering and leave without ordering anything at all. The key question, then, may not be how many options people are given, but whether they have the knowledge and tools to make sense of them. Stores and websites that help customers sort and filter products may therefore be able to offer wide selections without driving buyers away.

choices: make shoppers more willing to spend
improve the quality of the products sold
encourage stores to lower their prices
paralyze rather than empower decision-makers
questions.why: 品数が多いと人は集まるが、買う人は少ない、という実験結果のまとめ。選択肢の多さが決断を妨げる（paralyze）。もっとお金を使う・品質が上がる・値下げは実験の内容と関係ない。

choices: Under closer scrutiny, however
As a result of this popularity
In much the same way
For precisely this reason
questions.why: 前は「考えが広まった」、後ろは「再現が難しかった・効果はほぼゼロ」。逆の流れなので however を含む「よく調べると、しかし」。As a result・In much the same way・For precisely this reason は順接で合わない。

choices: have already made similar purchases
are shopping with experienced friends
lack a clear sense of what they prefer
know the products extremely well
questions.why: 直後の例で、専門家はすぐ絞れるが初心者は戸惑う、とある。だから「何が好みか分かっていない時」に圧倒される。know the products extremely well は専門家側で逆。他の2つは本文に根拠が無い。

sets.passage:
Keeping Time on the Rails

Until the middle of the nineteenth century, most towns set their clocks according to local solar time, declaring it noon when the sun reached its highest point in the sky. Because the sun's position changes as one travels east or west, towns only a short distance apart often kept slightly different times. A town fifty miles to the west of another might be several minutes behind it. In most communities, a clock on the town hall served as the official reference, and residents adjusted their pocket watches to match it. For centuries, ( 1 ). Few people traveled far in a single day, and a journey by horse-drawn coach was so slow that a difference of a few minutes hardly mattered.

The arrival of the railways changed this situation dramatically. Trains could cover in an hour a distance that had once taken a full day, and passengers relied on printed timetables to plan their journeys. At first, each railway company simply used the time kept at its own headquarters, so a single station might display several clocks showing different times for different lines. Travelers who misread a timetable could easily miss a connection, and the risk of collisions on shared tracks made accurate timekeeping a matter of safety as well as convenience. Railway companies ( 2 ), dividing the land into broad zones in which every clock showed the same hour.

The change was not welcomed by everyone. Some critics complained that time belonged to the sun, not to businesses, and argued that ordinary people should not have to adjust their lives to suit train schedules. A number of towns stubbornly continued to keep their own local time for years, and some public clocks were even fitted with two minute hands, one for local time and one for railway time. Over the following decades, however, standard time was ( 3 ). Schools, banks, and post offices gradually followed the railways' lead, and the second minute hand disappeared from public clocks. Today, most people would be surprised to learn that the hour on their watch was once a matter of local custom rather than a fixed, shared agreement.

choices: travelers complained constantly about the confusion
these discrepancies caused few practical problems
towns competed to keep the most accurate time
clocks were regarded as too expensive to own
questions.why: 直後に「1日に遠くへ行く人は少なく、馬車は遅いので数分の差は問題にならなかった」とある。だから時刻のずれは困らなかった。constantly complained は逆。正確さの競争・時計の値段は本文に無い。

choices: eventually agreed to adopt a common time
decided to stop publishing timetables
began building separate tracks for each line
allowed passengers to set their own schedules
questions.why: 後ろの「地域を大きな帯に分け、その中の時計はすべて同じ時刻」から、共通の時刻を採用したと分かる。時刻表をやめる・路線ごとの線路・乗客が決める、は混乱の解決にならない。

choices: woven so deeply into daily life that few questioned it
abandoned in favor of the older system
used only by the railway companies themselves
considered a threat to public safety
questions.why: However で反対派の話から転じ、「今では昔は地域ごとだったと知ると驚く」と続く。だから標準時が生活に深く根付いた。旧制度に戻った・鉄道だけが使った・安全への脅威、は最後の文と矛盾する。

sets.passage:
The Return of the Beaver

In many parts of Europe, beavers were hunted almost to extinction for their fur and meat, and by the early twentieth century only a few small populations remained. In recent decades, however, conservation groups have reintroduced the animals to rivers where they had been absent for hundreds of years. Ecologists often describe beavers as "ecosystem engineers" because few other creatures reshape their surroundings so thoroughly. Their sharp front teeth, which never stop growing, allow them to cut through trunks far thicker than their own bodies. By felling trees and building dams from branches and mud, a single family of beavers can transform a narrow stream into a series of ponds and marshes.

These changes ( 1 ). The still water behind a dam provides breeding grounds for frogs and insects, which in turn attract birds and bats. Fallen trees create open, sunny areas where new plants can take root, and the dead wood offers shelter for beetles and fungi. Researchers have also found that beaver ponds store water during dry periods and slow the movement of water after heavy rain, releasing it gradually rather than all at once. In some places, streams that once dried up every summer now flow throughout the year.

Not everyone, however, is pleased to see beavers return. Farmers have complained that dams cause water to spread onto their fields, damaging crops and making the ground too soft for machinery. Landowners have also lost valuable trees, and blocked drainage pipes can cost a great deal to repair. Some residents also worry that the animals may wander into towns and block the channels that carry water under roads. ( 2 ), several regions have introduced programs that pay for devices that control water levels behind dams, as well as compensation for landowners whose property is damaged. In extreme cases, wildlife officers are permitted to move a beaver family to a more suitable location. Supporters of reintroduction admit that these measures require time and money, but they argue that the ecological benefits far outweigh the costs. As one ecologist put it, the long-term success of the project may depend less on the beavers themselves than on ( 3 ).

choices: mostly harm the fish living downstream
make the rivers too cold for wildlife
benefit a wide range of other species
are usually reversed within a few years
questions.why: 直後に、カエル・昆虫・鳥・コウモリ・植物・甲虫など多くの生き物が得をする例が並ぶ。下流の魚に害・川が冷たくなる・数年で元に戻る、は本文に無い。

choices: Regardless of these complaints
Long before beavers returned
Contrary to farmers' wishes
In response to such conflicts
questions.why: 前の段落は農家・地主の被害。空所の後は水位の調整装置や補償の制度。被害への対応なので「こうした対立に応えて」。Regardless（気にせず）・Contrary to farmers' wishes は逆の意味。Long before（帰ってくるずっと前）は時期が合わない。

choices: the amount of fur the animals produce
people's willingness to share the landscape with them
the speed at which they build their dams
the number of predators in the area
questions.why: 段落全体が人間との対立と、その折り合いの付け方の話。成功は「ビーバー自身より、人間が土地を共有する気があるか」で決まる。毛皮・ダムの速さ・天敵の数は段落の話と関係ない。

sets.passage:
The Illusion of Understanding

Most adults feel reasonably confident that they understand how ordinary objects such as zippers, flush toilets, and bicycles work. In a well-known series of studies, researchers tested this confidence directly. Participants first rated their understanding of several everyday devices on a seven-point scale. They were then asked to write a detailed, step-by-step explanation of how each device functions, and afterward to rate their understanding again. The second ratings were dramatically lower than the first, and some participants admitted that they could not even explain how the device actually worked. Faced with the task of describing exactly how the parts of a zipper fit together, many participants realized that their knowledge ( 1 ).

Psychologists call this phenomenon the "illusion of explanatory depth." One reason it arises, they suggest, is that people tend to mistake familiarity for comprehension. Having used an object thousands of times, we feel that we know it well, even though we have never had to think about its inner workings. We also rely heavily on knowledge stored elsewhere, in manuals, online, or in the minds of experts, and we rarely notice where our own understanding ends and theirs begins. ( 2 ), the illusion is not limited to mechanical devices. When participants were asked to explain a complex economic process, such as how changes in interest rates affect house prices, their confidence fell in much the same way, and the opinions they expressed afterward tended to be less extreme.

Interestingly, this effect seems to depend on the type of explanation requested. In related experiments, people who were simply asked to list the reasons for their opinions did not become more moderate; if anything, they held their views more firmly than before. Only when they tried to describe step by step how something would actually happen did they recognize the gaps in their knowledge. One possible explanation is that listing reasons allows people to repeat familiar arguments, whereas explaining a process forces them to confront details they have never considered. Some researchers therefore suggest that teachers and managers who want to encourage more thoughtful discussion should ( 3 ).

choices: was far more detailed than they had expected
had been gained mainly from reading manuals
consisted of little more than a vague impression
grew steadily with each new attempt
questions.why: 詳しく説明しようとして理解度の自己評価が大きく下がった、という結果のまとめ。知識は「ぼんやりした印象にすぎなかった」。思ったより詳しかった・回を追うごとに増えた、は逆。説明書で得た、は本文に無い。

choices: Perhaps more surprisingly
As a direct result
For precisely this reason
In sharp contrast
questions.why: 前は機械の話、後ろは「機械に限らず経済の話でも同じことが起きた」という意外な広がり。因果（As a direct result / For precisely this reason）でも、対比（In sharp contrast）でもない。

choices: encourage people to defend their opinions as firmly as possible
avoid discussing complicated subjects in groups
ask people to list as many reasons for their views as they can
ask people to explain how something works rather than why they hold a view
questions.why: 理由を挙げさせると考えがかえって固くなり、仕組みを順を追って説明させた時だけ知識の穴に気づいた。だから「なぜそう思うか」ではなく「どう働くか」を説明させるとよい。理由を挙げさせる（3つ目）は逆効果の方。

sets.passage:
Shipping Ice Around the World

In the early nineteenth century, a few merchants in the northeastern United States had what seemed like an absurd idea: cutting blocks of ice from frozen lakes in winter and shipping them to hot countries thousands of kilometers away. Early attempts were costly failures. Much of the cargo melted during the voyage, and in tropical ports, few people had any idea what to do with ice. Some shipments arrived only to find that there was nowhere cool enough to store them. To build demand, traders handed out free samples and showed bar owners how to serve chilled drinks. Over time, customers who had once regarded ice as a curiosity came to ( 1 ).

The greatest technical challenge was insulation. Traders experimented with many materials before discovering that sawdust, a waste product of lumber mills that was available almost for free, kept ice frozen remarkably well when packed tightly around the blocks. Specially built icehouses with thick double walls allowed ice to be stored for months in warm climates. With these improvements, losses during long voyages fell sharply. By the middle of the century, ice cut from lakes in New England was being sold in ports across the Caribbean, South America, and even India, and the trade employed thousands of workers each winter.

( 2 ), the industry that had grown so impressively began to decline. During the second half of the century, inventors developed machines that could produce ice artificially using compressed gases. At first, machine-made ice was expensive and often regarded with suspicion, but as the technology improved, ice factories could be built close to the customers they served. Natural ice, by contrast, depended on cold winters, and a mild season could leave traders with nothing to sell. Moreover, as cities grew, many of the lakes from which ice was cut became polluted. Refrigerated railway cars and household iceboxes, meanwhile, came to rely on the steadier supply that factories could offer. Although natural ice was harvested in some places until the early twentieth century, the trade eventually disappeared. Its influence, however, lasted. By teaching people around the world to expect cold drinks and fresh food, it ( 3 ).

choices: fear that it might damage their health
regard it as a necessity of daily life
prefer drinks served at room temperature
use it mainly for medical purposes
questions.why: 無料の試供品や冷たい飲み物の出し方を教えて需要を作った結果、珍しい物だった氷が「生活に欠かせない物」になった。健康への不安・常温を好む・医療用は、需要が育った流れと合わない。

choices: Thanks to these improvements
In the same way
For this reason
Within a few decades, however
questions.why: 前の段落は大成功、この文は「衰え始めた」。逆の流れなので however。Thanks to these improvements・For this reason は順接、In the same way は似た話を続ける時に使う。

choices: made machine-made ice unnecessary for most families
slowed the growth of cities in warm countries
helped create the demand on which modern refrigeration was built

The Value of Dead Wood

For much of the twentieth century, foresters in many countries regarded fallen branches and dead trees as signs of poor management. Dead wood was thought to harbor insects and diseases that might spread to healthy trees, and removing it made forests look tidy and made timber easier to harvest. As a result, in carefully managed forests, dead wood was often cleared away almost as soon as it appeared, and forest workers were sometimes paid according to the amount of dead material they removed. Ecologists now argue that this practice ( 1 ).

The reason is that dead wood is far from lifeless. As a fallen trunk slowly decays, it provides food and shelter for an enormous range of organisms. Fungi and bacteria begin to break down the wood, and they are followed by beetles, ants, and other insects, which in turn attract the birds and small mammals that feed on them. Some species of beetle can survive only in wood that has reached a particular stage of decay. In some European forests, researchers estimate that around a quarter of all forest species depend on dead wood at some point in their lives. Even standing dead trees are valuable, since woodpeckers carve nest holes in them that are later used by owls and bats. ( 2 ), as decaying logs gradually release nutrients into the soil, they help to feed the next generation of trees.

Following these findings, forest managers in several regions have changed their approach. Instead of removing every dead tree, they now leave a certain volume of dead wood on the ground, and some even create it deliberately by removing a ring of bark from a few living trees. Such efforts must be balanced against other concerns, however. Standing dead trees near hiking trails can fall without warning, and in commercial forests, wood that is left to decay is wood that cannot be sold. Moreover, simply leaving dead wood in a forest is not always enough. Because many specialized species can travel only short distances, they are unable to reach suitable logs that are scattered too far apart. For this reason, ecologists recommend that managers ( 3 ).

sets.passage:
The Hot Hand Debate

Basketball players, coaches, and fans have long believed in the "hot hand," the idea that a player who has made several shots in a row is more likely than usual to make the next one. In the 1980s, a group of psychologists set out to test this belief. They analyzed thousands of shots taken by professional players and found that the chance of success after a series of hits was no higher than after a series of misses. Their conclusion was that the hot hand ( 1 ). People, they argued, are simply poor at recognizing randomness and tend to see streaks where none really exist. The finding surprised many players, some of whom insisted that they could feel when they were on a streak.

The study became one of the best-known examples of a "cognitive bias," and for three decades it was widely cited in textbooks and popular books on decision-making. Fans who continued to believe in the hot hand were often presented as examples of irrational thinking. ( 2 ), the original analysis contained a subtle mathematical error. Many years later, two economists pointed out that when one examines a limited sequence of shots and selects only those that follow a streak of hits, a hidden bias is created. Because of this bias, a player with no hot hand at all would actually be expected to perform slightly worse after a streak. Finding no difference, therefore, suggested that players really did perform better than chance after making several shots in a row.

The debate has not been completely settled. Some researchers point out that even if the hot hand exists, the effect appears to be small, and players and coaches may still overestimate it, for example by passing the ball too often to a teammate who has just made a few shots. Others argue that the size of the effect may vary greatly from one player to another. Nonetheless, the episode is often cited as a valuable lesson for scientists. It shows that a finding which seems to confirm a popular theory about human error can itself ( 3 ).

choices: applied only to the most experienced players
could be developed through careful training
was nothing more than an illusion
explained why some teams won more often than others

For this reason
In much the same way
As it turned out, however

sets.passage:
Learning Through Productive Failure

In a typical mathematics classroom, lessons follow a familiar pattern. The teacher first demonstrates a method, works through several examples, and then asks students to practice similar problems on their own. This approach is efficient, and it allows students to experience success quickly. In recent years, however, a number of education researchers have argued that it may be reversing the most effective order of learning. They advocate an approach known as "productive failure," in which students are given challenging, unfamiliar problems before receiving any instruction on how to solve them. Proponents argue that this initial struggle, far from being wasted time, prepares the mind to learn. Predictably, most students fail to find the correct solution. Only afterward does the teacher explain the standard method, often by comparing it with the students' own attempts.

Supporters point to a study conducted at the Westbrook Institute of Education, in which two groups of thirteen-year-olds were taught how to measure the spread of a set of data. One group received a conventional lesson followed by practice, while the other spent the first half of the lesson struggling to invent its own measures. When both groups were tested a week later, their performance on routine calculation questions was almost identical. On questions that required students to explain why a formula worked, or to apply it to an unfamiliar situation, however, the group that had struggled first scored considerably higher. The researchers suggested that generating several flawed solutions had forced students to draw on what they already knew and made them aware of the gaps in their understanding. As a result, when the correct method was finally presented, they could appreciate what problem it solved rather than simply memorizing its steps.

Critics caution that the benefits of struggle are far from guaranteed. For failure to be productive, the initial problem must be carefully designed: difficult enough to require genuine thought, yet accessible enough that students can make several reasonable attempts. Students who lack basic background knowledge may be unable to generate any meaningful ideas at all, and for them, a long period of confusion can lead to frustration and a loss of confidence rather than deeper understanding. Teachers, too, report that the approach is demanding. They must resist the urge to rescue struggling students, manage the anxiety that some students feel when they cannot find an answer, and explain to parents why lessons seem to involve so much getting things wrong. Lessons built around initial failure also take longer to plan and to teach, which can be a serious drawback in schools where teachers must cover a crowded curriculum before national examinations.

Most researchers therefore recommend using productive failure selectively. Rather than replacing conventional instruction altogether, it may be most valuable when introducing a small number of core concepts that students will build on for years. Some researchers also recommend that teachers openly discuss with students why the struggle is part of the plan, so that failure is seen as a normal step rather than a personal shortcoming. Used in this way, a carefully planned failure may turn out to be one of the most useful experiences a student can have.

questions.q: What distinguishes the "productive failure" approach from conventional mathematics instruction?
choices: Students practice a large number of similar problems until they can solve them without errors.
Teachers deliberately give students incorrect methods so that they learn to spot mistakes.
Students are asked to work on problems before they have been taught a method for solving them.
Students are allowed to choose which problems they want to work on during the lesson.

sets.passage:
The Ocean's Twilight Zone

Between roughly 200 and 1,000 meters below the surface of the ocean lies a region that scientists call the mesopelagic zone, or, more evocatively, the "twilight zone." Sunlight here is too faint to support plant growth, yet the zone is home to an astonishing variety of animals, from tiny shrimp-like crustaceans to fish no longer than a finger that produce their own light. Because it is so difficult and expensive to study, the twilight zone remains one of the least understood environments on the planet. Most of what is known about it comes from brief expeditions using specialized nets, cameras, and underwater robots.

One of its most remarkable features is a daily movement of animals that some researchers describe as the largest migration on Earth. Each evening, enormous numbers of fish and other creatures rise toward the surface to feed on plankton under the cover of darkness. Before dawn, they descend again to the dim depths, where they are less visible to predators. Some animals travel several hundred meters each way, a journey comparable to a person walking many kilometers twice a day. This journey has consequences far beyond the animals themselves. Plankton near the surface absorb carbon from the atmosphere, and when migrating animals eat them and then release waste or die at depth, much of that carbon is carried down into the deep ocean, where it can remain for centuries. The twilight zone, in other words, plays a significant role in regulating the planet's climate.

For many years, scientists believed that the total mass of fish in the zone was relatively modest. These estimates were based largely on catches made with research nets. More recently, however, surveys using sound waves to detect fish have produced figures many times higher. Researchers now suspect that the earlier surveys greatly underestimated the population, partly because many twilight zone fish are able to sense approaching nets and swim away from them. Other species are so fragile that they are torn apart inside the nets, leaving little trace in the catch.

These new estimates have attracted the attention of the fishing industry. Twilight zone fish are generally too small and oily to be eaten by people, but they could be ground into fishmeal and oil for use in fish farming, an industry that has grown rapidly as demand for seafood has risen. Supporters argue that this vast, untouched resource could reduce pressure on overfished species closer to the surface. Several countries have already shown interest in issuing licenses for experimental fishing. Many marine scientists, however, urge caution. They point out that so little is known about the zone's food webs that it is impossible to predict how large-scale fishing would affect them. If the number of migrating animals fell sharply, less carbon might be transported to the deep ocean, and the consequences for the climate could be serious. Moreover, many larger animals, such as tuna and whales, depend on twilight zone species for food. For now, the scientists argue, the priority should be to understand this hidden world before deciding whether it can safely be exploited.

choices: It occurs mainly because the animals are searching for warmer water at night.

It helps transfer carbon from the surface of the ocean to much greater depths.
It is the main reason that plants are unable to grow in the zone.

sets.passage:
Designing Cities for the Ear

For most of the twentieth century, city planners treated sound as a form of pollution. Noise from traffic, construction, and industry was measured in decibels, and the goal of policy was simple: reduce the numbers. Laws limited how loud machines could be, and walls were built along highways to block the roar of passing vehicles. These measures brought real benefits, since long-term exposure to loud noise has been linked to sleep problems and stress. In many cities, maps were produced showing which streets exceeded legal limits, and money was spent on quieter engines and road surfaces.

In recent decades, however, a growing number of researchers have argued that decibel readings tell only part of the story. Advocates of what is known as the "soundscape" approach point out that people do not experience sound simply as volume. The splash of a fountain or the chatter of a busy market can be just as loud as nearby traffic, yet most people find such sounds pleasant or even calming. What matters, these researchers argue, is how people perceive and interpret the sounds around them, and that perception depends heavily on context, expectations, and the meaning people attach to a sound. A dog barking in the distance may go unnoticed in a farming village but feel intrusive in a quiet apartment late at night.

One often-cited example is the redesign of Marlow Square, a busy public space in a mid-sized city. Rather than attempting to block the noise of the surrounding roads, designers added a series of fountains, planted trees to attract birds, and arranged seating so that visitors faced away from the traffic. Measurements taken after the project showed that overall sound levels in the square had barely changed. Yet in surveys, residents described the area as far more relaxing than before, and the number of people who used the square during their lunch breaks more than doubled. Visitors also reported that they were less aware of the traffic, even though it was still clearly audible. For supporters, the results showed that cities can improve people's experience of sound without the enormous expense of eliminating noise at its source.

Not everyone is convinced. Some public health experts warn that pleasant sounds may merely mask harmful noise rather than reduce it, and that the body may continue to react to traffic noise even when the mind no longer notices it. Others worry that the soundscape approach could provide officials with an attractive excuse to avoid more costly measures, such as rerouting heavy vehicles or installing quieter road surfaces. Neighborhoods located beside busy highways, they argue, need genuine reductions in noise, not decorative fountains.

Most researchers in the field see the two approaches as complementary rather than competing. Reducing harmful noise remains essential, but once the worst problems have been addressed, thoughtful design can help turn a merely tolerable environment into one that people actively enjoy. Several cities have begun to involve residents in "sound walks," in which participants note which sounds they value and which they would like to see removed.

choices: It aims to eliminate all sounds from public spaces in cities.
It focuses on how people perceive sounds rather than only on how loud they are.
It relies on stricter laws that limit the volume of machines.
It measures noise more accurately than earlier decibel readings.

sets.passage:
Darkness Under Threat

For most of history, the night sky above towns and villages was dark enough for people to see thousands of stars. Today, however, artificial light from streetlights, buildings, and advertising signs has spread so widely that a large proportion of the world's population lives under skies that never become truly dark. Astronomers were among the first to complain about this "light pollution," since the glow from cities makes it difficult to observe faint objects in space. In recent decades, however, biologists have begun to argue that the problem is far more serious than an inconvenience for stargazers.

Many living things have evolved to depend on the regular cycle of day and night. Moths and other night-flying insects, for example, appear to use the moon and stars to keep a steady course, and when they encounter a bright lamp, they often circle it until they are exhausted or are caught by predators. Some researchers believe that artificial light may be one of several factors behind the decline in insect numbers reported in many regions. Even a single lamp, some studies suggest, can affect insects living hundreds of meters away. The effects can spread through entire ecosystems. In one field study, scientists placed streetlights in meadows that had previously been dark and found that flowers in the lit areas were visited far less often by night-flying pollinators. Because many of the same flowers are also visited by bees during the day, the researchers had expected daytime visits to make up the difference. Instead, the lit plants produced noticeably fewer seeds.

Birds are affected as well. Many species migrate at night, and bright lights on tall buildings can draw them off course, causing them to waste energy or to collide with windows. In cities, some songbirds have been observed singing in the middle of the night near streetlights, and certain species begin breeding earlier in the spring than birds in darker areas. Whether this early start is harmful is not yet clear, but scientists worry that it may cause chicks to hatch before the insects their parents feed them have become plentiful.

Unlike many other forms of pollution, light pollution can be reduced almost immediately and often at little cost. Lamps can be fitted with shields so that they shine downward rather than into the sky, and they can be dimmed or switched off late at night when few people are around. The color of light also matters. Studies suggest that the bluish-white light produced by many modern LED lamps attracts more insects than warmer, amber-colored light. Several towns have already replaced their streetlights with warmer models and installed sensors that brighten lamps only when someone passes by. In some places, regulations now require new outdoor lighting to meet such standards.

Such changes are not always welcomed, however. Some residents worry that darker streets will feel less safe, even though research on the link between lighting and safety has produced mixed results. Supporters of dark-sky policies argue that the solution is not to remove lighting altogether but to use it more thoughtfully, putting light only where and when it is needed, and in the right amount.

choices: Bees visited the lit flowers more often during the day, which increased seed production.
Night-flying insects were drawn into the lit meadows from the surrounding dark areas.
Flowers in the lit areas began to open only during the daytime.
Visits by daytime pollinators did not make up for the loss of visits at night.

sets.passage:
Sizing Up the Customer

Until the nineteenth century, most clothing in Europe and North America was made to measure. Wealthy people had their garments sewn by tailors and dressmakers, while poorer families made their own clothes at home or bought second-hand ones. The idea of walking into a shop and buying a ready-made coat in a standard size would have seemed strange to most people. The shift toward ready-to-wear clothing began, perhaps surprisingly, with armies. When governments needed to supply huge numbers of uniforms quickly, it became impractical to measure every soldier individually. Manufacturers therefore began producing uniforms in a limited range of sizes based on chest measurements, and when the fighting ended, they applied the same methods to clothing for ordinary men. Standard sizes also made it possible to produce clothes in large factories and sell them in distant shops, greatly lowering their price.

Women's clothing proved much more difficult to standardize. Men's jackets and shirts could be sized reasonably well using one or two measurements, such as chest and neck, but women's garments of the period were more closely fitted and varied greatly in style. In the early twentieth century, manufacturers each used their own measurements, and a dress labeled as a particular size by one company might be much larger or smaller than a dress with the same label from another. To solve this problem, large-scale surveys were carried out in which thousands of women were measured. The results, however, were less useful than had been hoped. Because the volunteers had not been selected carefully, they did not represent the population as a whole, and the systems based on the surveys fit many customers poorly.

The situation became even more confusing in later decades because of a practice known as "vanity sizing." Companies discovered that customers were more likely to buy clothes labeled with a smaller size number, so they gradually made garments larger without changing the labels. Because the changes happened slowly, few customers noticed them at the time. As a result, a dress of a given size today may be considerably larger than one with the same number sold fifty years ago, and sizes may vary widely from brand to brand. Some shoppers find that they need to try on three different sizes before finding one that fits.

This inconsistency has real costs. Online retailers, in particular, receive enormous numbers of returns from customers whose purchases did not fit, and processing them is expensive as well as environmentally harmful because of the additional transportation and packaging involved. Some estimates suggest that a large share of all clothing bought online is eventually sent back. Some companies are now experimenting with software that asks customers to enter their height and weight, or to upload photographs of themselves, and then recommends a size for each item. Others have proposed abandoning single size numbers altogether and labeling garments with actual body measurements instead. Whether such approaches will catch on remains to be seen, but they reflect a growing recognition that a system inherited from nineteenth-century uniform makers no longer serves today's diverse customers well.

questions.q: According to the passage, how did armies contribute to the development of ready-made clothing?
choices: They required soldiers to buy their own uniforms from local tailors.
They taught tailors how to take more accurate measurements.
The need to produce many uniforms quickly led to the use of standard sizes.
They encouraged women to wear clothing similar to military uniforms.
questions.why: 第1段落：大量の軍服を急いで用意するため、一人ずつ測るのをやめ、胸囲で決めた少数のサイズで作った。それが一般の男性服にも使われた。自分で買わせた・測り方を教えた・女性の服、は本文に無い。

choices: The people who were measured did not accurately reflect the general population.
Manufacturers refused to share the results with one another.
Too few women agreed to take part in the surveys.
The surveys measured only one or two parts of the body.
questions.why: 第2段落：参加者を注意して選ばなかったので、全体を代表していなかった。参加者は数千人なので「少なすぎた」は誤り。1〜2か所だけ測るのは男性服の話。結果を共有しなかった、は本文に無い。

questions.q: What does the author suggest about the current system of clothing sizes?
choices: Vanity sizing has made it easier for online shoppers to choose the right size.
It is more consistent than the system used fifty years ago.
New technology has already solved most of the problems it causes.
Its inconsistency creates costs for businesses and for the environment.
questions.why: 第4段落：サイズがばらばらなので返品が多く、費用がかかり、輸送や包装で環境にも悪い。見栄サイズは選びにくくした原因で逆。50年前より一貫している、も逆。新しい技術は「広まるかはまだ分からない」。

sets.passage:
The Value of Effort

Many people have spent an entire afternoon assembling a bookcase from a flat-pack kit, struggling with confusing instructions and tiny screws, only to feel unusually proud of the finished product. Psychologists who have studied this experience suggest that it reflects a general tendency: people place a higher value on objects they have helped to create, even when their contribution has been small and the result is far from perfect. The same pattern has been observed with many kinds of homemade objects, from knitted scarves to simple pieces of furniture.

In a series of experiments, researchers asked participants to fold paper animals by following simple instructions. Afterward, the participants were asked how much they would be willing to pay for their own creations. They were then shown similar animals folded by skilled experts and asked how much they would pay for those. Remarkably, the participants were willing to pay nearly as much for their own clumsy creations as for the experts' work, and they expected other people to value their animals highly as well. Other people did not share this view, however; when neutral observers were asked to bid on the participants' creations, they offered very little. The effect also had limits. When participants were given instructions so difficult that they could not complete the task, or were asked to take apart what they had built, their creations no longer seemed especially valuable to them. It appeared that effort had to end in success for it to increase an object's value.

Researchers have proposed several explanations for this phenomenon. One is that completing a task gives people a sense of competence, and the object serves as a reminder of their achievement. Another is that people tend to justify the time and energy they have invested; if something required a great deal of work, they reason, it must be worth having. These explanations are not mutually exclusive, and both processes may operate at the same time. Some studies suggest that the effect is strongest among people who are especially eager to feel capable.

The tendency has important practical consequences. Businesses have long understood that customers who take part in creating a product may value it more. According to a popular story, early instant cake mixes, which required only the addition of water, sold poorly until manufacturers changed the recipe so that customers had to add a fresh egg. Historians have questioned whether the story is accurate, but the principle behind it has been widely applied, from furniture that customers assemble themselves to websites that allow shoppers to design their own sneakers.

The same tendency can also cause problems. In workplaces, employees who have developed an idea may overvalue it and resist evidence that a colleague's proposal is better. Managers who want to make sound decisions may therefore need to have projects evaluated by people who were not involved in creating them. Understanding why we love what we build, in other words, can help us recognize when that love is leading us astray. It may also explain why organizations sometimes keep investing in failing projects simply because so much work has already gone into them.

questions.q: What did the paper-folding experiments show?
choices: Participants valued the experts' animals much more highly than their own.
Participants valued their own creations far more highly than other people did.
Neutral observers were willing to pay high prices for the participants' animals.
Participants' creations became more valuable to them after they took them apart.
questions.why: 第2段落：自分の不格好な作品に専門家の作品とほぼ同じ値を付けたが、中立の人はほとんど払わなかった。専門家の作品をずっと高く評価、は逆。分解すると価値が下がったので4つ目も逆。

questions.q: According to the passage, what is one condition for the effect to occur?
choices: The person must receive help from an expert while working.
The task must take a long time to complete.
The finished product must be of high quality.
The person must succeed in completing the task.
questions.why: 第2段落の最後：努力が成功で終わらないと価値は上がらない（完成できなかった・分解した時は効果が消えた）。仕上がりは「完璧には程遠くても」よいので3つ目は誤り。専門家の助け・長い時間は条件として書かれていない。

questions.q: Why does the author mention workplaces?
choices: To show that employees work harder when they design their own products.
To argue that companies should let customers assemble products themselves.
To illustrate how the tendency can lead people to make poor judgments.
To suggest that managers should be more involved in developing new ideas.
questions.why: 最終段落：自分の考えを高く見すぎ、同僚のより良い案を受け入れない＝判断を誤る例。関わっていない人に評価させるべき、と言っているので「管理職がもっと関わる」は逆。客に組み立てさせる話は前の段落。

sets.passage:
Navigating by Magnetism

Every year, billions of birds travel thousands of kilometers between their breeding grounds and the places where they spend the winter, often returning to exactly the same nesting site year after year. How they manage to find their way has puzzled scientists for centuries. Some small songbirds weighing less than twenty grams cross entire deserts and seas without stopping. Birds are known to use several kinds of information, including the position of the sun during the day and the pattern of the stars at night. Experiments have shown, however, that many species can also navigate under cloudy skies, when neither the sun nor the stars are visible. This observation led researchers to suspect that birds possess a sense that humans lack: the ability to detect the earth's magnetic field.

Early evidence for this magnetic sense came from experiments with caged songbirds. During the migration season, such birds become restless and tend to hop in the direction in which they would normally fly. When researchers used electric coils to alter the magnetic field around the cages, the birds changed the direction of their hopping accordingly. Later studies suggested that the birds were not simply detecting north and south, as a compass needle does. Instead, they appeared to sense the angle at which the magnetic field lines meet the earth's surface, an angle that changes with distance from the equator. This information could tell a bird roughly how far north or south it is.

Exactly how birds detect the magnetic field remains controversial. For many years, one popular theory held that tiny particles of a magnetic mineral in birds' beaks acted like miniature compass needles connected to the nervous system. More careful investigation, however, revealed that many of these particles were found in a type of blood cell involved in fighting infection rather than in nerve cells, and the theory lost much of its support. A second theory proposes that the sense is located in the eye. According to this view, a protein in the retina undergoes a chemical reaction when struck by light, and the outcome of that reaction is affected by the magnetic field. If this is correct, birds may literally see the magnetic field, perhaps as a pattern of light and shade laid over their normal vision. In support of this idea, some experiments have found that the magnetic sense works only when a certain amount of light is available.

Understanding this ability is not merely of scientific interest. Researchers have discovered that weak electromagnetic noise from electronic equipment, at levels far below those considered harmful to humans, can disrupt the magnetic orientation of birds. In one study, birds kept in wooden huts in a city lost their sense of direction but regained it when the huts were covered with aluminum screens that blocked the noise. Such findings suggest that human activity may be affecting migrating birds in ways that are invisible and that, until recently, no one had expected. Some scientists have therefore called for more research into how such noise might be reduced in places where birds rest during migration.

questions.q: Why did researchers begin to suspect that birds can detect the earth's magnetic field?
choices: Birds were observed flying in circles when the sun was shining brightly.
Birds that lost their way at night were found to have damaged eyes.
Caged birds refused to move when the stars were hidden.
Many birds could find their way even when the sky was covered by clouds.
questions.why: 第1段落：太陽も星も見えない曇りの日でも多くの鳥が方角を知る。これが磁気を感じる感覚を疑うきっかけ。晴れた日に回る・目の傷・星が隠れると動かない、は本文に無い。

questions.q: What did later studies suggest about birds' magnetic sense?
choices: It may allow birds to estimate how far they are from the equator.
It works in exactly the same way as a compass needle.
It is used only by birds that are kept in cages.
It is less reliable than the positions of the sun and stars.
questions.why: 第2段落：磁力線が地面と交わる角度を感じているようで、その角度は赤道からの距離で変わる＝南北どのくらいの位置か分かる。方位磁針と同じ、は「ただ南北を知るのではない」と否定。他の2つは本文に無い。

questions.q: What happened to the theory that magnetic particles in birds' beaks act as compasses?
choices: It was confirmed when the particles were found inside nerve cells.
It lost support when many of the particles turned out to be in other kinds of cells.
It was combined with the theory that birds sense magnetism through their eyes.
It was proven by the experiments using aluminum screens.
questions.why: 第3段落：粒子の多くは神経の細胞ではなく、感染と戦う血液の細胞にあったので、支持を失った。神経細胞で見つかった、は逆。目の説とは別の説として紹介。アルミの覆いは電磁ノイズの実験。
