sets.passage:
Do Trees Talk to Each Other?

Over the past three decades, few ideas in ecology have captured the public imagination as powerfully as the "wood wide web." According to this idea, the trees in a forest are linked underground by vast networks of fungi that grow around and into their roots. These fungi, known as mycorrhizal fungi, are said to act like a living internet, allowing trees to share sugars, water, and even chemical warning signals with one another. In the most popular versions of the story, large, old "mother trees" use the networks to feed their own seedlings growing in the shade, and dying trees pass their remaining resources on to their neighbors. Some versions even suggest that trees can recognize their relatives and send them a larger share of resources than they send to unrelated neighbors. The forest, in this view, is less a collection of competing individuals than a cooperative community.

It is not difficult to see why the idea became so popular. It appeared in best-selling books, award-winning documentaries, and even feature films, and it offered a moving picture of nature that seemed to challenge the image of the forest as a place of ruthless competition for light and nutrients. For many readers, the notion that trees nurture their young and support their sick neighbors was not only fascinating but also deeply comforting. Some foresters and conservation groups began citing the networks as a reason to protect old trees, arguing that cutting them down would destroy the hubs on which the whole forest depended.

In recent years, however, a number of scientists have begun to question whether the evidence supports such dramatic claims. One team of researchers carefully reviewed several dozen field studies that had been cited in support of the wood wide web. Their conclusions were striking. First, they found that there was surprisingly little direct evidence that fungal networks connecting many trees are common in real forests. Proving that two trees are linked by the same fungus is technically difficult, and only a handful of studies had attempted to do so, most of them in a small number of forest types. Moreover, the fungal species involved can change over time, so a link observed in one season may not exist in the next. Second, although some experiments had shown that carbon could move from one tree to another, it was often unclear whether it had traveled through the fungal network or by some other route, such as through the soil. And even where transfer did occur, the amounts were usually too small to make a meaningful difference to the receiving tree.

The third finding concerned the claim that networks help seedlings survive. When the reviewers examined experiments that tested this idea, they found that the results were remarkably inconsistent. In some studies, seedlings connected to older trees grew better; in others, they grew worse; and in many, there was no noticeable difference at all. The reviewers argued that the positive results had been widely publicized, while the negative or neutral ones had been largely overlooked.

This last point raised a broader concern about how scientific ideas spread. The reviewers analyzed how often the original studies had been cited in later research papers, and they discovered a clear pattern. Studies that appeared to support the wood wide web were cited far more often than those that did not, and when they were cited, their findings were frequently described in stronger terms than the original authors had used. A cautious statement that carbon "may" move between trees under certain laboratory conditions, for example, might become a confident claim that trees "share" food in nature. Over time, the reviewers suggested, these small exaggerations accumulated until the public story bore only a loose resemblance to the underlying evidence.

Not all scientists accept this critique. Some researchers who helped develop the idea argue that the reviewers set an unreasonably high standard of proof, and that the overall pattern of evidence, though incomplete, still points toward meaningful connections between trees. They also note that forests are enormously complex, and that the absence of evidence in a few studies does not prove that networks are unimportant. They also point out that seedlings planted in sterilized soil, without access to fungi, often struggle to survive. Both sides, however, agree on several basic points: mycorrhizal fungi are essential to the health of most trees, they exchange nutrients with their host plants, and far more research under natural conditions is needed.

The debate also has practical implications. If the strongest claims about mother trees turn out to be exaggerated, does that mean old trees are less valuable than conservationists have argued? Not necessarily. Large, old trees store huge amounts of carbon, provide habitats for countless species, and influence the conditions in which younger trees grow, regardless of whether they feed them through fungal networks. The lesson of the controversy, some ecologists suggest, is not that the forest is a simple battleground after all, but that policies are on firmer ground when they rest on what has actually been demonstrated rather than on the most appealing version of a story. Some researchers add that the episode should encourage scientists and journalists alike to use more modest language when describing new findings to the public.

questions.q: What made the idea of the "wood wide web" so appealing to the general public?
choices: It proved that trees compete fiercely with one another for light and nutrients.
It was based on a large number of studies conducted in many types of forest.
It suggested that old trees could be cut down without harming the forest.
It portrayed forests as caring communities, a picture many people found emotionally moving.
questions.why: 第2段落：木が子を育て弱った仲間を支える、という像が魅力的で心を慰めるものだった。競争の場というイメージを覆したので、激しい競争を証明したは逆。研究が多かった、は第3段落で否定。老木を切ってよい、も逆。

questions.q: According to the review described in the passage, what was one problem with the evidence for carbon transfer between trees?
choices: The amounts of carbon transferred were usually large enough to harm the receiving tree.
Researchers had found that fungi prevent carbon from moving through the soil.
It was often uncertain whether the carbon had passed through fungi or along another path.
Most experiments had been carried out on trees that were already dying.
questions.why: 第3段落：炭素が別の木へ移っても、菌のネットワーク経由か土など別の経路かが分からないことが多かった。量は「意味のある差を生むには少なすぎた」ので、害を与えるほど多いは逆。他の2つは本文に無い。

questions.q: What did the reviewers discover when they examined how the original studies had been cited?
choices: Studies that did not support the idea were usually cited first in later papers.
Supportive findings were cited more often and were often described more confidently than their authors intended.
Most researchers had refused to cite studies about mycorrhizal fungi at all.
The original authors had made stronger claims than later researchers repeated.
questions.why: 第5段落：支持する研究ほど多く引用され、しかも元の著者より強い言い方で紹介された（may → share）。支持しない研究が先に引用された、元の著者の方が強く言った、は逆。

questions.q: Which of the following statements would the author of the passage most likely agree with?
choices: Even if some claims about tree networks were exaggerated, there are still good reasons to protect old trees.
The debate has shown that mycorrhizal fungi play no important role in forest health.
Scientists who developed the wood wide web idea have now abandoned it completely.
Forest policy should be based on whichever version of a scientific story is most popular.
questions.why: 最終段落：老木は炭素を蓄え多くの生き物のすみかになるので、ネットワーク説が誇張でも価値は残る。菌は健康に不可欠と両者が同意しているので「役割なし」は誤り。提唱者は反論しているので放棄していない。最後の文は「魅力的な話より実証されたことに基づく方がよい」なので4つ目は逆。

sets.passage:
Bringing a Language Back

On the small, windswept island of Varn, lying some forty kilometers off the northern coast of the mainland, a language called Ostrani was once spoken in nearly every home. For centuries, islanders used it to bargain at the harbor, to sing at weddings, and to name the hundreds of rocks, currents, and fishing grounds that surrounded their coast. By the end of the twentieth century, however, fewer than three hundred fluent speakers remained, almost all of them over the age of sixty. Linguists who visited the island predicted that within a generation Ostrani would disappear entirely.

The decline had not been caused by any single event. As the island's fishing industry shrank from the 1950s onward, many young people moved to the mainland in search of work, and the national language became essential for anyone hoping to find a job or continue their education. Schools on the island taught exclusively in the national language, and teachers often advised parents that speaking Ostrani at home would only confuse their children. Many parents, wanting the best possible future for their sons and daughters, took this advice. They continued to speak Ostrani with their own parents and neighbors but switched to the national language when addressing their children. Within a single generation, the chain of transmission from parent to child had been broken. The children grew up understanding some Ostrani but rarely speaking it, and their own children grew up knowing almost none. Over time, the language also came to be associated with poverty and an old-fashioned way of life, which made some young islanders reluctant to use it even when they could.

The turning point came in the 1990s, when a group of islanders, many of them the children of those who had stopped speaking the language at home, formed an association to revive it. They began by recording elderly speakers telling stories and describing traditional crafts, creating an archive of several thousand hours of conversation. Volunteers transcribed the recordings and added translations, so that learners could study them at home. Their most ambitious project, however, was a "language nest," a preschool in which children between the ages of two and five spent their days with older speakers who used nothing but Ostrani. The idea was based on the observation that young children acquire languages most easily through everyday interaction rather than formal lessons. At first, only six families enrolled their children. Today, the nest has a waiting list, and its graduates can continue their education in Ostrani at a primary school that teaches most subjects in the language.

For adults, the association developed a different approach. In its "master and apprentice" program, a fluent elder and a younger learner commit to spending at least ten hours a week together, cooking, fishing, or repairing nets while speaking only Ostrani. Participants say the program has benefits that go beyond language. Elders who had once felt that their knowledge was worthless report a renewed sense of purpose, and learners describe forming relationships with people they might otherwise never have met. The program has also produced practical knowledge: several apprentices have compiled dictionaries of fishing terms and place names that had never been written down.

The revival has not been free of tension, however. Because Ostrani had never had a standard written form, the association needed to create one in order to produce textbooks and teaching materials. In doing so, it chose spellings and grammatical forms based mainly on the variety spoken in the island's largest village. Elders from other parts of the island sometimes complain that the young people who learn from these textbooks speak a version of the language that sounds artificial to them, and a few have refused to take part in the program altogether. Others have proposed allowing several spellings to coexist, though teachers say this would make materials far harder to prepare. Some young learners, for their part, feel discouraged when older speakers correct them constantly or tell them that their Ostrani "is not the real thing." Linguists who study language revival say that such disagreements are common, and that the emergence of "new speakers" whose language differs from that of earlier generations is a natural part of the process rather than a sign of failure.

Measuring the success of the revival is not straightforward. According to the association's most recent survey, around nine hundred people on the island can now hold a conversation in Ostrani, triple the number of thirty years ago. Yet most of them use the language mainly at school, at association events, or online, and only a few dozen families speak it as their main language at home. Some supporters worry that Ostrani is becoming a language that people study rather than one they live in. The association has responded by organizing weekly gatherings in cafés and at the harbor, where speakers of all ages are encouraged to use the language informally. Others are more optimistic. They point out that the first generation of language-nest graduates is now beginning to have children of its own, and that several of these young parents have chosen to raise their children in Ostrani. If that trend continues, the chain that was broken half a century ago may finally be restored.

questions.q: Why did the number of children speaking Ostrani decline?
choices: Many parents spoke the national language to their children because they thought it would give them better opportunities.
The government passed a law that banned the use of Ostrani on the island.
Elderly speakers refused to teach the language to people outside their families.
Children found Ostrani too difficult to learn because it had no written form.
questions.why: 第2段落：仕事や教育に国の言葉が必要になり、先生の助言もあって、親が子どもには国の言葉で話すようになった。法律での禁止は書かれていない。お年寄りの拒否・書き言葉が無いから難しい、も理由として出てこない。

questions.q: What was a key feature of the language nest established by the association?
choices: Children studied Ostrani grammar in formal lessons before they started school.
Young children spent their days with older people who spoke to them only in Ostrani.
Parents were required to attend classes with their children every morning.
Children listened to recordings of elders instead of speaking with teachers.
questions.why: 第3段落：2〜5歳の子どもが、Ostrani だけを使う年配の話者と1日を過ごす。正式な授業ではなく日常のやり取りで覚える、という考え。保護者の出席・録音を聞くだけ、は本文に無い。

questions.q: Why have some elders been critical of the young people learning Ostrani?
choices: They believe the young people spend too little time practicing with apprentices.
They think the language should be written using the national language's spelling.
They are worried that the young people will leave the island to find work.
They feel that the standardized version taught in textbooks does not sound authentic.
questions.why: 第5段落：教科書は一番大きな村の言い方を基準にしたので、他の地域のお年寄りには人工的に聞こえる。練習時間・つづりの方式・島を出る心配は、批判の理由として書かれていない。

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the Ostrani revival is true?
choices: Linguists believe the appearance of new speakers shows that the revival has failed.
The master and apprentice program has mainly benefited the young learners rather than the elders.
Although more people can now speak Ostrani, relatively few families use it as their main language at home.
The number of people able to converse in Ostrani has stayed about the same for thirty years.
questions.why: 最終段落：話せる人は約900人と3倍になったが、家庭で主に使うのは数十家族だけ。言語学者は新しい話者を「失敗の印ではない」と言う。弟子制度はお年寄りにも生きがいを与えた。人数は3倍で「同じ」ではない。

sets.passage:
The Trouble with Open Offices

For much of the twentieth century, office workers in many countries spent their days in private rooms or in small cubicles separated by partitions. From the 1990s onward, however, a growing number of companies began tearing down these walls and moving their employees into large, open spaces where desks were arranged in long rows or clusters. Supporters of the open-plan office made two main arguments. The first was financial: by removing walls and fitting more desks into the same area, companies could greatly reduce the amount of space they needed to rent. The second was cultural. Open offices, it was claimed, would encourage employees to talk to one another more often, break down barriers between departments and levels of seniority, and allow ideas to flow freely. Managers who sat among their staff rather than behind closed doors would seem more approachable, and chance encounters between people from different teams would spark new forms of collaboration.

The financial benefits were real, but the cultural claims proved harder to verify. For years, evidence about the effects of open offices came mainly from employee surveys, which consistently found that workers in open spaces complained more about noise and lack of privacy than those in private offices. Such surveys, however, measured how people felt rather than how they actually behaved. A company might reasonably accept some grumbling about noise if the new layout genuinely increased cooperation.

To address this gap, a team of researchers studied two companies that were preparing to move from traditional offices to open-plan layouts. Before and after the move, volunteers wore small electronic badges that recorded when they were speaking face to face with colleagues, and the researchers also collected data on the employees' emails and instant messages. The results were the opposite of what the designers of the open offices had predicted. After the walls came down, face-to-face interaction fell by roughly two-thirds, while the volume of electronic messages rose considerably. Rather than chatting more, employees appeared to protect themselves from constant observation by putting on headphones, keeping their eyes on their screens, and contacting nearby colleagues by email.

The researchers suggested that this behavior was a natural human response. In a space where everyone can see and hear everything, people may feel that any conversation will disturb others or be overheard, and so they avoid starting one. Privacy, in other words, may be a precondition for openness rather than its enemy. Other studies have found that the constant background noise of open offices makes it harder to concentrate on complex tasks such as writing or analysis, and some research has linked open-plan layouts to higher rates of sick leave, perhaps because illnesses spread more easily when many people share the same air.

Defenders of open offices argue that these findings should not be overstated. Studies of a small number of companies, they point out, may not apply to all organizations, and the outcome may depend heavily on how a space is designed and managed. An open office with high ceilings, sound-absorbing materials, and clear rules about noise may function very differently from a crowded room with hard floors and no quiet areas. Moreover, some kinds of work genuinely benefit from being able to see and hear colleagues. In a newsroom, for example, information must be shared instantly, and overhearing a conversation can be an advantage rather than a distraction.

Partly in response to these debates, many companies have adopted what is known as "activity-based working." Instead of assigning each employee a permanent desk, these offices provide a variety of spaces designed for different purposes: open areas for teamwork, small enclosed rooms for phone calls or concentrated work, and comfortable lounges for informal meetings. Employees are expected to move between these spaces depending on what they are doing at any given time. In principle, this approach combines the advantages of open and private layouts. In practice, results have been mixed. Some workers enjoy the freedom to choose, but others report spending a significant amount of time each morning searching for a free desk, and many people settle in the same spot every day regardless of the task they are performing. When companies reduce the total number of desks to save money, the competition for quiet spaces can become intense.

The spread of remote work has added yet another dimension to the discussion. With many employees now working from home for part of the week, offices are increasingly used for activities that are difficult to do online, such as meetings, training, and building relationships. Some experts argue that this shift strengthens the case for open, flexible spaces designed mainly for interaction, with concentrated work done at home. Others caution that not every employee has a quiet place to work at home, and that offices should continue to provide spaces where people can focus without interruption.

What the history of the open-plan office suggests, perhaps, is that there is no single ideal layout. The mistake made by many companies was not that they chose open spaces, but that they assumed a change in physical design would automatically produce a change in human behavior. Workplaces seem to function best when employees have some control over their surroundings and can choose between being visible and being undisturbed.

questions.q: What was one reason supporters gave for introducing open-plan offices?
choices: They would make it easier for managers to monitor employees' productivity.
They would reduce the amount of noise that employees had to deal with.
They would encourage communication between people in different positions and departments.
They would allow companies to spend more money on office equipment.

sets.passage:
Placebos Without Deception

For centuries, doctors have known that patients sometimes feel better after receiving a treatment that contains no active ingredient. A sugar pill, an injection of salt water, or even a fake operation can, under the right conditions, reduce pain, improve sleep, or ease the symptoms of digestive disorders. This "placebo effect" has long been regarded as both a nuisance and a mystery. It is a nuisance because, in order to show that a new drug genuinely works, researchers must prove that it produces better results than a placebo, and a strong placebo response can make an effective medicine appear useless. It is a mystery because no one fully understands how a substance with no medical properties can produce real changes in how people feel.

Research over the past few decades has begun to clarify some of the mechanisms involved. Brain-imaging studies have shown that when people who have been given a placebo for pain expect relief, their brains release natural pain-reducing chemicals. Expectation appears to be central. Patients who are told that a treatment is likely to be effective tend to respond more strongly than those who are told that its effects are uncertain. Even the appearance of a treatment matters: in several studies, capsules were perceived as more powerful than tablets, and pills in brand-name packaging produced stronger effects than identical pills in plain packaging. The relationship between patient and practitioner also seems to play a role. In one experiment involving patients with a long-term digestive condition, those who received fake acupuncture from a warm, attentive practitioner reported greater improvement than those who received the same fake treatment from a practitioner who was polite but distant.

For a long time, it was assumed that the placebo effect depended on deception. If patients knew that their pill contained nothing but sugar, the reasoning went, their expectation of improvement would disappear, and so would the effect. This assumption created an ethical problem. Although many doctors have admitted in surveys that they occasionally prescribe treatments mainly for their psychological effect, such as vitamins for patients who do not need them, deliberately misleading patients is widely considered a violation of their right to make informed decisions about their own care. Some doctors once argued that a small amount of deception was justified if it helped patients, but this view has become far less accepted as medicine has placed greater emphasis on patients' rights.

Recent studies, however, have challenged the assumption that deception is necessary. In a series of trials, patients suffering from conditions such as chronic back pain were given what researchers call "open-label placebos." The patients were told clearly that the pills contained no active ingredient, but they were also told that placebos had been shown to produce improvements through processes in the body and mind, and they were encouraged to take the pills regularly. Surprisingly, many of these patients reported significant improvements compared with patients who received no pills at all. In some trials, the benefits were substantial. Several participants said that they had expected nothing to happen and were astonished by the results.

How can a pill work when the patient knows it is fake? Researchers are still debating the answer. One possibility is that the ritual of taking a pill, which people have performed countless times when they were ill and later recovered, triggers a learned response that operates partly outside conscious awareness, much as the smell of a favorite food can make the mouth water. Another is that open-label placebos encourage patients to pay attention to their symptoms in a more hopeful way, noticing small improvements that they might otherwise have overlooked. A third suggestion is that simply doing something about a problem, rather than waiting passively, may reduce the anxiety that often makes symptoms feel worse.

Not everyone is convinced. Critics point out that most open-label trials have been small and that, because patients know whether they are receiving a pill, the studies cannot be "blinded" in the usual way. Patients who agree to take part may also be unusually open to the idea that placebos can help, which could exaggerate the results. Furthermore, most of the improvements reported have involved conditions in which symptoms are measured by asking patients how they feel, such as pain or tiredness. There is little evidence that placebos, open-label or otherwise, can shrink tumors, lower blood sugar, or cure infections. Some doctors worry that enthusiasm for placebos could lead patients to delay seeking effective treatment for serious illnesses.

Even so, many researchers believe that the study of placebos holds valuable lessons for medicine as a whole. If expectations, rituals, and the quality of the relationship between doctor and patient can influence how people feel, then these factors are likely to affect the success of real treatments as well. A doctor who takes the time to listen to a patient and explain a treatment clearly may be doing more than simply being polite. From this perspective, the goal is not so much to prescribe fake pills as to make sure that every genuine treatment is delivered in a way that makes the most of the body's own capacity for healing.

It can make it difficult to show that a new drug is effective.
It makes patients expect doctors to spend more time with them.

sets.passage:
How Cats Came to Live with Humans

Of all the animals that share our homes, the cat is perhaps the most puzzling. Dogs, horses, and cattle were domesticated by people who deliberately selected animals for useful traits, such as the ability to herd sheep, pull heavy loads, or produce large quantities of milk. Cats, by contrast, perform few tasks that people need, rarely follow commands, and in many cases still hunt and breed largely as they please. For this reason, some researchers describe cats as only "semi-domesticated," and many scientists now believe that, rather than being tamed by humans, cats largely domesticated themselves.

According to this view, the story began roughly ten thousand years ago, when people in the Near East started to farm. Early farmers stored large amounts of grain, and these stores attracted mice and rats. The rodents, in turn, attracted wildcats from the surrounding countryside. Wildcats that were less afraid of people could take advantage of this rich new food supply, and over many generations, populations living near villages became increasingly tolerant of human company. Farmers, for their part, probably had good reason to welcome animals that kept pests under control. No one needed to capture or breed the cats deliberately; the relationship developed because it benefited both sides.

Archaeological evidence supports the idea that this relationship is very old. On an island in the eastern Mediterranean, archaeologists discovered a grave, thought to be around 9,500 years old, in which a person had been buried together with a young cat. Since wildcats are not native to the island, the animal or its ancestors must have been brought there by boat, suggesting that people already valued cats enough to carry them across the sea. Egyptian paintings created thousands of years later show cats sitting under chairs and wearing collars, indicating that by then they had become household companions as well as pest controllers. Some researchers caution, however, that a single grave cannot tell us whether cats were common companions at the time or whether this case was unusual.

More detailed insights have come from genetics. In one large study, researchers analyzed DNA from the remains of more than two hundred cats found at archaeological sites across Europe, Africa, and Asia, covering a period of about nine thousand years. The results suggested that domestic cats spread in two major waves. The first accompanied early farmers as agriculture expanded from the Near East into neighboring regions. The second came much later, when cats from Egypt spread rapidly around the Mediterranean and beyond. Because cats from this second wave have been found at ports and along trade routes, the researchers concluded that they were probably carried on ships, where they would have been valued for protecting food supplies and cargo from rodents.

The genetic study also revealed something surprising: for most of their history, domestic cats looked very much like their wild relatives. The blotched "tabby" coat pattern familiar to many cat owners today, for example, did not become common until the Middle Ages. Selective breeding for particular colors, coat lengths, and body shapes, which has produced the wide variety of modern breeds, began only within the past two hundred years or so. Compared with dogs, whose appearance and behavior have been changed dramatically by thousands of years of selective breeding, cats remain genetically close to wildcats, and the two can still breed with each other where their ranges overlap.

This closeness raises interesting questions about how domestication changes animals. Some researchers have proposed that domesticated mammals share a set of features, including smaller brains, floppy ears, shorter faces, and patches of white fur. They believe these features may be linked to changes in a group of cells that develop very early in the embryo. Domestic cats do have somewhat smaller brains than wildcats, and white patches are common, but they show these traits less strongly than many other domesticated species. Researchers who study cat behavior point out that the most important changes may be ones that cannot be seen at all. Domestic cats are far more tolerant of other cats and of humans than wildcats are, and they appear to have developed special ways of communicating with people. Some studies suggest, for instance, that adult cats meow far more often to humans than to other cats, and that individual cats may adjust their meows depending on how their owners respond.

Understanding the history of cat domestication is not merely of academic interest. The same qualities that allowed cats to live alongside humans without being fully controlled by them have also made them a challenge for conservation. Domestic cats that roam freely kill large numbers of birds and small mammals each year, and on some islands they have contributed to the decline of native species. Some communities have responded by encouraging owners to keep their cats indoors, especially at night, although such measures remain controversial among cat lovers. At the same time, wildcat populations in parts of Europe are threatened partly because they interbreed with domestic cats and gradually lose their genetic distinctiveness. Managing these problems requires recognizing that the cat occupies an unusual position between the wild and the domestic worlds, one that it has held, largely on its own terms, for thousands of years.

questions.q: Why do many scientists believe that cats "domesticated themselves"?
choices: Early farmers captured wildcats and trained them to hunt mice.
Cats were selected by humans for their ability to follow commands.
Wildcats were brought into villages because people wanted them as pets.
Wildcats that tolerated people benefited from living near human food stores.

sets.passage:
The Changing Role of Zoos

For most of their history, zoos existed mainly to entertain. In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, city zoos displayed as many exotic species as possible, often in small, bare cages that gave visitors a clear view of the animals but gave the animals little room to move. Animals were captured from the wild in large numbers, and many died within a few years of arriving. Over the past several decades, however, many zoos have attempted to reinvent themselves. Leading institutions now describe their main missions as conservation, education, and scientific research, and they have replaced cages with larger enclosures designed to resemble natural habitats. Critics, however, continue to question whether keeping wild animals in captivity can be justified at all.

The strongest argument in favor of modern zoos concerns endangered species. A number of animals that had disappeared from the wild, or nearly so, survived only because small populations were kept and bred in captivity. In several cases, zoos and related breeding centers have successfully returned animals to their natural habitats once the threats that had driven them toward extinction were reduced. Zoos have also become important sources of funding for conservation in the wild, using part of the money they earn from ticket sales to protect habitats, train local wildlife rangers, and support research in the countries where endangered species live. Supporters argue that without such contributions, many conservation programs would struggle to survive. Researchers based at zoos have also contributed knowledge about animal health and reproduction that is now used by scientists working in the wild.

Critics respond that these success stories, while real, involve only a small proportion of the animals that zoos keep. Most species on display are not endangered, and many of those that are endangered are not part of any program to return them to the wild. Large, wide-ranging animals pose a particular problem. Elephants, polar bears, and big cats naturally travel great distances, and research has found that some individuals kept in zoos show signs of stress, such as pacing back and forth or swaying from side to side for long periods. Although enclosures have improved, critics argue that no zoo can provide enough space for an animal that might cover dozens of kilometers in a single day in the wild. For such species, they say, the case for captivity is especially weak.

Zoos also claim to educate the public, inspiring visitors to care about wildlife and to support conservation. Here the evidence is mixed. Some surveys have found that visitors leave with a greater understanding of biodiversity and a stronger sense that they can help protect it. Other studies, however, suggest that many visitors spend only a few seconds in front of each enclosure and pay little attention to information signs, treating a visit primarily as a pleasant day out with their families. Researchers have also noted how difficult it is to measure whether a visit to the zoo actually changes people's behavior, for example by encouraging them to donate to conservation groups or to make environmentally friendly choices, rather than simply changing what they say in a survey.

In response to such criticism, some zoos have changed which animals they keep. Several have stopped housing elephants or have sent them to large sanctuaries, focusing their resources instead on smaller species that can be cared for more effectively, such as frogs, insects, and reptiles. Many of these species are seriously threatened in the wild, and they can often be bred successfully in relatively small spaces. Such species rarely attract crowds in the way that elephants and lions do, however, so these zoos have had to find new ways of drawing visitors. Other zoos have extended their work beyond their own grounds, operating field stations and research programs in natural habitats. Some conservationists have even proposed that the zoo of the future should look less like a park for viewing animals and more like a combination of breeding center, research laboratory, and visitor center.

Not everyone is satisfied with these reforms. Some animal-welfare groups argue that the existence of zoos sends the message that it is acceptable to keep wild animals for human enjoyment, regardless of how well they are treated. They believe that resources would be better spent protecting habitats directly, so that animals do not need to be kept in captivity at all. Zoo supporters respond that habitat protection and captive breeding are not alternatives but complementary strategies; for species whose habitats are disappearing rapidly, a population kept safely in captivity may provide crucial insurance while longer-term solutions are developed.

The debate is unlikely to be resolved soon, partly because the two sides often start from different values. For some, the welfare of each individual animal is the most important consideration; for others, the survival of entire species matters more. What does seem clear is that the traditional zoo, built mainly to display as many impressive animals as possible, is becoming harder to defend. Zoos that wish to justify their existence in the twenty-first century will need to show, with clear evidence, that the animals in their care benefit from being there and that their work makes a measurable difference to the survival of species in the wild.

questions.q: How have many zoos changed over the past several decades?
choices: They have shifted their focus toward conservation, education, and research.
They have increased the number of animals captured from the wild.
They have stopped charging visitors for admission.
They have replaced natural-looking enclosures with smaller cages.

In laboratories around the world, scientists are now able to grow real animal meat without raising and slaughtering animals. The process begins with a small sample of cells taken from a living animal. These cells are placed in large steel tanks filled with a nutrient-rich liquid, where they multiply until they form tissue that can be shaped into products such as burgers or chicken nuggets. Several start-up companies have already offered cultivated meat to diners in a small number of restaurants, and investors have poured large sums of money into the industry.

Supporters believe that cultivated meat could solve several problems at once. Conventional livestock farming requires vast areas of land for grazing and for growing animal feed, and it is responsible for a significant share of the world's greenhouse gas emissions. Producing meat in tanks, they argue, could dramatically reduce the land and water needed to feed a growing global population. In addition, animal welfare groups point out that the technology would allow people to continue eating meat without causing animals to suffer.

Skeptics, however, question whether these promises can be fulfilled. At present, producing cultivated meat is extremely expensive, partly because the nutrient liquid in which the cells grow is costly to make. Scaling up production to the level of an industrial meat plant would require enormous investments in equipment and energy, and some researchers have calculated that, if that energy comes from fossil fuels, the environmental benefits could be much smaller than advertised. There are also doubts about whether consumers will accept the product. In surveys, many people say they find the idea of meat grown in a factory unnatural or even disturbing.

Farmers' organizations have raised further concerns. They worry that if cultivated meat becomes popular, rural communities that depend on livestock farming could lose their main source of income, and traditional knowledge about raising animals could disappear. Some have called for strict labeling rules so that consumers can clearly distinguish between conventional and cultivated products. Whether the technology becomes a common part of people's diets or remains a costly curiosity may depend as much on public attitudes and government regulation as on scientific progress.

A growing number of companies now use computer software to help them decide which job applicants to interview. These programs scan résumés for relevant skills and experience, and some go further, analyzing applicants' answers to online questionnaires or even their facial expressions and tone of voice in recorded video interviews. For employers that receive thousands of applications for a single position, such tools promise to make the hiring process far faster and cheaper.

Advocates argue that automated screening can also make hiring fairer. Human recruiters, they point out, are influenced by unconscious biases. They may favor applicants who attended the same university as themselves or who have names that sound familiar, and they may judge candidates differently depending on how tired they are at the end of the day. A well-designed program, by contrast, applies the same criteria to every applicant. Some companies that have adopted such tools report that they now interview a more diverse range of candidates than before.

Critics, however, warn that automated systems can reproduce and even magnify the very biases they are supposed to remove. Many programs learn what a "good" employee looks like by studying data about a company's past hires. If those hires were mostly drawn from a narrow group, the software may learn to rank similar applicants more highly and quietly screen out others. Because the programs' decision-making processes are often complex and kept secret by the companies that sell them, it can be extremely difficult for rejected applicants to find out why they were turned down, or to challenge the decision.

There are also concerns about the methods used in some systems. Experts in psychology have questioned whether facial expressions or speech patterns recorded during a short video can reveal anything meaningful about a person's ability to do a job. In response to such criticism, some governments have begun to consider rules that would require employers to inform applicants when software is used, and to have the systems tested regularly for unfair outcomes. Others argue that the final decision on whom to hire should always be made by a human being.

Many large cities have long struggled with heavy traffic in their central districts. Traffic jams waste time, raise transportation costs for businesses, and contribute to air pollution. In an attempt to address these problems, a number of cities have introduced what are known as congestion charges. Under such schemes, drivers must pay a fee to enter the city center during busy hours, with cameras recording the license plates of vehicles that cross the boundary. Drivers who fail to pay within a set period receive a fine, while residents of the zone and some essential vehicles may be given discounts.

Supporters say the results have been impressive. In cities that have adopted congestion charges, the number of vehicles entering the center has often fallen significantly within the first year, and travel times for buses and delivery vehicles have improved. Air quality in central streets has also tended to get better. These are short courses, often offered online by universities, technology companies, or professional associations, that certify a person's skills in a specific area, such as data analysis or project management. Many can be completed in a few weeks or months and cost only a fraction of a traditional degree.

Supporters argue that micro-credentials are well suited to a rapidly changing job market. As new technologies transform industries, workers increasingly need to update their skills throughout their careers rather than relying on what they learned in their early twenties. Supporters also point out that micro-credentials can open doors for people who cannot afford the time or money required for a full degree, such as working parents or those living far from a university. Because they are offered by so many different organizations, their quality varies enormously, and employers may find it hard to judge what a particular certificate actually represents. Some surveys suggest that, although employers say they value specific skills, many still prefer to hire applicants with traditional degrees. There is a risk, critics say, that workers will spend money on a series of short courses that do little to improve their job prospects.

Educators have expressed another concern. A university education, they argue, is not only about acquiring job-related skills. It also aims to develop critical thinking, communication, and the ability to understand complex problems from different perspectives, abilities that are difficult to teach in a short online course. Some universities are now trying to combine the two approaches by allowing students to build up micro-credentials that can later be counted toward a full degree. Whether this model becomes widespread may depend on how much trust employers and students come to place in these new forms of certification.

Today, anyone can order a genetic testing kit online for a modest price. After sending a small sample of saliva to the company, customers receive a report that may describe their ancestry, their likelihood of developing certain medical conditions, and even traits such as how their bodies respond to caffeine. Millions of people around the world have now used these services.

Many customers find the results valuable. Learning that they have an increased risk of a particular disease can motivate people to change their diet, exercise more, or arrange regular medical checkups, potentially allowing problems to be detected at an early stage. For others, information about their family origins has led to a deeper understanding of their identity, and in some cases, people have even discovered relatives they never knew existed.

Medical experts, however, caution that such tests can be misleading. Most common diseases are influenced by many genes as well as by lifestyle and environment, so a report stating that a person has a "slightly elevated risk" may be of little practical use. Some customers who receive worrying results experience considerable anxiety, while others who receive reassuring results may wrongly conclude that they do not need to take care of their health. Unlike tests ordered by doctors, these kits are usually not accompanied by professional advice to help people interpret what they mean, and few companies explain the limits of their predictions in a way that ordinary customers can easily understand.

Privacy is another major concern. Genetic data reveals information not only about the person who provided the sample, but also about their parents, children, and other relatives, none of whom agreed to the test. Companies may share data with research partners, and critics worry that it could one day be used by insurers or employers. Although some companies promise to protect their customers' information, the rules governing how genetic data can be stored and shared differ widely between countries. Many experts are therefore calling for clearer regulations before the technology becomes even more widespread.

Business owners in the tourism industry also worry that visitors will choose cheaper destinations instead, leading to lost income and jobs.

There are also questions about how the money is spent. In some places, residents complain that tourist tax revenue disappears into general government budgets rather than being used to address the problems caused by tourism. Experts suggest that taxes are most likely to win public support when the authorities clearly explain how the money will be used and when they are combined with other measures, such as limits on short-term rentals or systems that require visitors to book entry to popular sites in advance.

For these reasons, many experts believe that the four-day week is unlikely to replace the traditional schedule completely in the near future. Instead, it may become one of several flexible options, such as staggered hours or remote work, that employers use to meet the needs of different workers.
